In putting any such question or in replying to the same no argument or opinion is to he offered, nor any facts stated, except so far as may be necessary to explain the same. And in answering any such question the matter to which the same refers shall not be debated.
Comments upon this rule will be found in Bourinot's Parliamentary Practice, pp. 433 to 435. Among the comments made in that work as to the form in which questions may be put, I would quote the following: (a). ' 'A question has been refused a reply because it referred to a. matter of opinion', (b). 'A question should be simply and severely accurate in its allegations. If it is hypothetical it is objectionable and should not be answered . (c). 'It should not be ironical or c?nvey any imputation'. Members are reminded that it is the duty of certain officers of the House to point out to a member when any question is put in improper form and to communicate with the member in order that the notice may be properly amended. speechtext: Mr. GEORGE GORDON (Nipissing) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 85) to amend the Criminal Code.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT-THEFT OF SILVER ORE.
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT-THEFT OF SILVER ORE.
speechtext: This Bill is an exact duplicate of one passed by this House and buried in the Senate last session, owing, I believe, to that honourable body not being aware of the extensive illegal traffic which is being carried on at the silver regions of Nipissing and which the law as it now stands, fails to cope with. Valuable ore, in many cases, nearly pure silver is being carried away in the pockets of persons who dispose of it in one of two ways: (1) It readily passes ' current ' at the ' Blind Pigs ' in exchange for cash for drinks, principally as I believe the latter, or, (2) It can be sold to persons who are making a business of dealing in it. When the receiver has aecummulated a quantity he takes it to Toronto or elsewhere and sells it. The monthly losses to the mines are very large, the trade being a considerable one. It seems to be impossible to stop the business with the law as it at present is because it is practically impossible by examination of a piece of ore to tell from what mine it came,- and on any prosecution for recovering stolen ore the prosecutor is not able to technically prove the theft. What is desired is to put the receivers out of business; if that is done these thefts will cease. What is aimed at is to throw upon any person found in the possession of ore the onus of proving where he got it.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

ADJOURNMENT-LOSS OF LIFE ON LAKE ERIE.
speechtext:
I desire to discuss for a moment a matter of great public importance which, I take it would be in charge of the Marine and Fisheries Department. I would have put what I have to say in the form of an interrogation addressed to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Brodeur) had that hon. gentleman been in his place. But, as he is not present at the moment, I shall make a motion for leave to move the adjournment of the House for the purpose of the discussion. The subject I wish to refer to is the loss of life by the foundering of the car ferry steamer ' Bessemer No. 2' on Lake Erie, off Port Stanley harbour. Despatches received from Toronto state that the Canadian Pacific Railway car ferry has been wrecked opposite Port Bur-well. Forty members of the crew were on the boat, but from last accounts, it is hoped that these have been taken off. But the boat is a complete wreck and these forty lives were at least endangered. The mat-'
ter is of very serious and urgent public importance and I bring it to the attention of the House because I think the government has been remiss in not having proper marine signals either at Port Stanley, Port Burwell or Rondeau Harbour.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-LOSS OF LIFE ON LAKE ERIE.
speechtext: If the hon. member is going to discuss the matter, he must submit a motion.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT-LOSS OF LIFE ON LAKE ERIE.
speechtext:
I have a motion drawn for the purpose. I move:
That leave be granted to move the adjournment of the House to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, viz.:	The recent
loss of the railway ferry ' Bessemer No. 2,' on Lake Erie, off Port Stanley, in which at least thirty-eight lives are known to have been lost.

Motion agreed to.
Mr. MACDONELL moved the adjournment of the House for the purpose stated. He said: I desire to bring to the attention of the government, and especially of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, the great loss of life that occurred because of the foundering of the car ferry 'Bessemer No. 2.' At least thirty-eight of a crew were on the boat. As there is no passenger ferry across this part of the lake-or any part of the lake at this season -there is every reason to fear that a number of additional persons were on board that ferry as passengers. I am informed that, although there are these three harbours on the north shore of Lake Erie, harbours on which large sums of public money have recently been spent-I believe quite $250,000 at Port Stanley, $200,000 at Port Burwell, and large works going on at Rondeau-yet in all these cases there is no marine warning for incoming vessels. These are not ordinary harbours that are closed at the close of navigation; they are open all the year round, and these railway car ferries run to these three harbours from the south shore of the lake throughout the year. Therefore, additional precautions should be taken there by the government to protect navigation. I am informed that there are some lights at Port Stanley and Port Burwell, but at neither is there a fog horn or other means of giving a signal or answering a signal of distress .from the water. On the night on which the 'Bessemer No. 2' went down, involving this shocking loss of life, a number of the residents of Port Stanley Harbour state the whistle of the steamer was he^rd blowing signals of distress again and again out in the lake. There were no means of answering that vessel. I am informed that during the progress of the work on the pier in the last year or two on many occasions signals of distress were sounded by this very boat and there being no means of answering these signals the contractors who were

doing the work would send out one of their tugs to the entrance of the harbour to answer these signals of distress, in that way enabling the captain and pilot of the boat to locate the harbour entrance. What happened on this occasion, apparently, was that during a blinding snow storm, when marine men could not see more than a boat's length or two ahead, the ferry had no means of knowing when it was near the harbour. Lights were of no avail, what was needed was a fog horn or proper marine signal which would warn them where the entrance to the harbour was and would answer their signals of distress. There were no means provided at the harbour of Port Stanley and as a direct consequence of that this boat foundered because she could not make the harbour and in turning to make shelter, either up or down the lake, in the opinion of marine men, the cars broke loose and she turned over and sank to the bottom.
In the opinion of marine men that loss of life and property could have been avoided had there been proper signals there to warn the vessel of its approach to the harbour. Practically the same thing happens thirty miles away further down the lake at Port Burwell, where we find the wrecked Canadian Pacific railway ferry steamer with forty men in danger from Sunday last until at least yesterday afternoon. It is incumbent upon the government to protect shipping at these points and I wish to point out to the Minister of Marine that this is not a case where navigation closes and signals are not needed. It is just after the ordinary navigation closes that these signals are required, during the snowstorm season and the storm season when lights cannot be made out that a fog horn or other means of signalling is absolutely indispensable. I wish to point out that there was no such means of warning at any of these harbours. It would have cost very little money to install these warnings, the lighthouse keepers at these different harbours could turn on steam and start the fog horn or steam whistle without the extra expense of one man. Thus the signals could have been given had the government taken the precaution to have installed a proper machine to give the usual warnings to mariners. I hope the government will take this matter seriously into consideration and that not only at the ports mentioned but at all other ports where ferries cross in the winter they will take the proper means to see that warnings for navigation are installed. Otherwise what is the use of spending millions on harbours and places of refuge if their approach is made impossible for want of proper aids to navigation?

Mr. Speaker, in continuing the debate on the budget deliverance of the hon. the Minister of Finance, I do not purpose making any lengthy remarks or discussing a large number of subjects. I have no doubt that I voice the sentiment of the country in expressing the satisfaction that it gave the people of Canada to hear the financial statement of the hon. the Finance Minister and to know that the country was in such a happy financial condition. I doubt not but it will be accepted with pleasure and satisfaction generally. It proclaimed a buoyant and expanding revenue, which is always desirable where extensive work is to be done; increasing commerce, and that I am sure will please every citizen of Canada; busy industrial life and heavy expenditure, that will please some, and it will displease others; a rapidly growing debt with our credit not improving but rather the reverse. With regard to the last two features, there may be some exception taken, some would desire that we had not have reached the record which we have reached to-day. Last year has been, according to the budget deliverance, a record year in the history of Canada in many respects. It has been a record year with regard to collections from the people. We collected $85,000,000, the largest sum perhaps, with one exception, that was ever collected from the people of Canada. Therefore it was a record year in that regard. We' spent $126,000,000, the largest amount that has ever been spent in one year in the history of Canada. Therefore our expenditure was a record breaker as well. We increased the debt by $45,969,414, in one year. I believe there is only one other year in the history of Canada where the increase of debt was larger than it was last year, and only one. We spent $31,317,132 on the Transcontinental rail-51
way and the Quebec bridge. With regard to that, I made an observation at the time the hon. Minister of Finance said that we had spent for the current year $31,000,000; I asked the question if that was the railway which was to be built by the surplus of one year, and the Finance Minister's reply was 'I am afraid that was a pipe dream of my hon. friend'. Something imaginative rather than the reality. That statement was credited to this side of the House rather than to the source to which it properly belonged. Not desiring to infringe upon the right of others, I simply wish to refer to that statement in the 'Hansard' at the time it was made, so that the people of Canada may know that it was no pipe dream in the mind of the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule), or of any other member of this side of the House; but if pipe dream it was, it should be credited to the Prime Minister, end not to the member for East Grey. This is what the 'Hansard' says as the words of the Prime Minister when he was explaining the Transcontinental Railway Bill:
The sum total of money .to he spent by the government for the construction of that line of railway from Moncton to the Pacific ocean will be in the neighbourhood of '$12,000,000 or $13,000,000, and not a cent more. . . . Now, Sir, what is $13,000,000 in 1903? It is about the surplus of revenue over expenditure; the surplus for this year will pay for the construction of this road.
Therefore the pipe dream, if pipe dream there was, ought to be credited to the hon. the First Minister instead of to the member for East Grey. I wish the country also to think over the fact that we have spent over $59,000,000 on a road that was going to cost less than the surplus of one year, less than $16,000,000 and the road is not half built yet. I want the country to think over the fact that we have recently voted over $20,000,000 this year, and we spent $31,000,000 last year, and a large amount the year .before. So the people of Canada may understand whether they were misled by the pipe dreams of the government when they undertook this gigantic enterprise.
This is going to be a record session also, we are told. Well, I looked over the speech from the Throne to ascertain what there was in it that would indicate that it was going to be a record session, and I noticed that that speech deals with only one question that might be regarded as new matter, and that is Naval Defence. On that question, as the Bill is not before the House, I do not desire or intend to make any lengthy observations. But I may say in passing that the speech from the Throne rather indicated that the Bill would have been brought before parliament long ago, and I cannot understand why the delay at the present time. The Governor General said:



Two members of my government attended the Imperial Conference, called by His Majesty's government on the question of defence. A plan was adopted after consultation with the admiralty, for the organization of a Canadian naval service, on the lines of the resolution of the House of Commons of the 29th of March last. The papers will be immediately brought down, and a Bill introduced accordingly.
Well, I would take the language to mean forthwith after the papers had been brought down. But we have now passed five weeks of the session, and although the papers were brought down long ago there is no Bill yet. Now I have only to say with regard to that measure that in my judgment what Canada expects is that something should be done immediately and effectively. I am not going to pretend to say what it will be, but it did occur to me at the time that the speech was made that the observations of my hon. friend from North. Toronto pointed directly to what was perhaps the sentiment of the country on the question then. Therefore, in order that it may be a reminder to the House and the country, may I be permitted to refer to those observations, and that is the only remark I intend to make on the subject. The hon. member for North Toronto said:
To-day parliament stands at the gateway. It is not for me to say how grave it is, but I cannot brush it aside. To-day it impresses itself upon the gravest statesmen of the old country; to-day it appeals to Australia until public subscriptions are taken and the government is being importuned to do even more than its settled policy to meet the emergency; to-day little New Zealand gives one Dreadnought and offers a second, and to-day Canada faces that position of peril, that imperial emergency. Bet me say to my right hon. friend that if, after careful consideration, he proposes to this parliament a means for meeting that emergency adequately, by the gift of Dreadnoughts or the gift of money, this side of the House will stand beside him in thus vindicating Canada's honour and strengthening the empire's defence.
I have only to say that I believe the sentiment of the country remains to-day the same as when these observations^ were made, and that what Canada desires is immediate and. effective action, whatever that action may be. I might for a moment ask what accounts foT the good times that we have, the buoyant revenue and the general prosperity of the country as indicated by the budget deliverance? It is quite natural that the Finance Minister and his supporters would desire to have the country believe that in some way or other their conduct was responsible for these good times. What accounts for the favourable condition of affairs to-day? It is to be chiefly accounted for by the bountiful crop that we have had which brought a very large Mr. SPROULE.
return to the labours of the field, to the agriculturists, who represent about 45 per cent of the population, and if you can give a good return to 45 per cent of the people and they are well employed, thus doing good to them, you necessarily do good to the whole population. The large return for their labours obtained by a great number of the people, and the very heavy expenditure carried on by the government in public works and in other lines, involving the distribution of 126 millions amongst the people of Canada, would help to make good times whether that expenditure was wise or unwise, extravagant, profligate or economical. The exceptionally heavy expenditure on railways, canals, telegraph and other lines would naturally help to make good times. Then, there is the expenditure which took place in connection with corporations outside of the government. Railway building is carried on extensively in the country to-day. The three great transcontinental railway companies are extending their branch lines in every direction at a very rapid rate and this as well means a heavy expenditure in the country. It means employment for labour at remunerative wages, and, therefore, it is one of the elements that assist in bringing about these good times. Then, there is the heavy influx of immigrants who bring with them all the money they possess, as well as their settlers' effects, which money must be spent immediately on arrival to support themselves and those dependent on them with the necessaries of life and to provide an outfit for commencing operations in the new country and in the new home. This money must be spent immediately, and it means a very large additional expenditure in the country. This means as well a valuable additional market for the products of the country that we have to sell because it is usually a market in which the highest prices are paid. A heavy expenditure is required to provide implements and other things necessary to the outfitting of the new-comers. This means not only an increased market, but it means a home market which is always the best market to be had. It means an enhanced value for everything that is produced in the country and that has to be sold. Compare that with a few years ago. It is undoubtedly due to the law of supply and demand, to increased consumption in the country, to the increased numbers to help to create the demand. But, what have the government to do with benefits derived by the people from the large harvest? Nothing whatever. To what extent were they responsible for the increased prices that were obtained by the people of the country for what they sold? They were in no way responsible for it. These increased prices were due entirely to the law of supply and

demand, with which the government had no connection. These things help materially to make good times and in consequence we have the good times that we now enjoy. Our trade and commerce affords a number of examples, but I will only mention one item and that is the enhanced value of everything that the country had to sell last year as compared with previous years. To show what this means to the people of Canada I will mention three articles of export and give a comparison of the prices that were obtained for them last year with the prices that were obtained for the same commodities a few years previously. First, take the exports of wheat. In 1896 we exported 9,919,000 bushels and the farmers got in return, $5,771,000 in round figures. What was that per bushel? It was 581 cents per bushel. That was a very low figure. That could not possibly mean good times for the farmers. But, we take 1906 and we find that the farmers of Canada exported 49,137,000 bushels, in return for which they received $48,000,000. In other words, they got 98 cents per bushel for their grain, whereas, in 1896, they only got 581 cents per bushel. What had the government to do with that? Nothing in the world. It means to the agriculturists of Canada a greatly increased return over what they received a few years previously and, therefore, they were benefited to that extent. Take cured meats. In 1897 we exported
1,861,000	pounds, for which we got $84,000. In 1909 we exported 1,610,000 pounds; that is over 250,000 pounds less. But instead of getting only $84,000 the farmers got $123,911 for it, or $34,493 more for 250,000 pounds less than they got in 1897. What had the government to do with that? Nothing at all. It was due to the markets of the world. Then, I take cheese. In 1897 the farmers of Canada exported 164,220,000 pounds of cheese, for which they got $14,676,000. In 1909 they exported exactly the same number of millions, or 164,907,000 pounds of cheese, for which they received $20,384,000. What had the government to do with that? Nothing whatever. But, it helped to make good times. It helped to make the farmer's return more profitable, but it is not attributable to anything that has been done by the government. It is attributable to the law of supply and demand.
I do not propose to travel over very extensive ground or to engage in anything like an analytical criticism of the budget utterances of the Finance Minister, but 1 wish, very briefly, to direct attention to one particular line where I think the government have been very remiss in their duty, and in connection with that I was rather surprised at the observations of the minister in closing his budget speech. The Finance Minister announced that there will 51J
be no changes in the tariff this year, and he used the following language:
We have no tariff changes to propose on this occasion. It is not because we have entered a claim that the tariff is perfect. We have no doubt that wherever you have a custom tariff necessarily as full and intricate as ours has to be there will be room for criticism and certainly always room for demands for changes. But, we are of the opinion that it is not in the best interests of the country that there should be frequent changes. We believe that frequent tariff changes must have a disturbing influence on the interests of the country and we wish to have it generally understood that where there has been a general revision of the tariff as we had two years ago the government would not be disposed to make changes unless the need for them was very urgent indeed.
Language of somewhat the same kind was used by the Minister of Finance last year and the year before. Let me point out to him that one of the changes made in the tariff when it was revised some years ago, was a change which I have always regarded as unwise and injurious to the interests of the agricultural community who represent 45 per cent of our population, and also the woollen textile industries which were being rapidly developed in Canada; which gave employment to thousands of hands, which produced cheaper clothing than we can now obtain, and which gave a better market to the farmers of Canada for their wool. When we gave the British preference we struck a vital blow at the woollen industry. When the reduction was made in the tariff rate on woollen fabrics there were in Canada 207_ woollen mills operating at full time, employing a large number of people and paying them good wages. These mills had 624 sets of cards, 2,645 looms, and 194,086 spindles moving all the time. But, a few years after the British preference was introduced instead of having 270 mills in operation in Canada there were only 197, instead of having 624 sets of cards there were only 521, and instead of having 2,654 looms there were only 1,706. That is the result of the tariff changes which the Minister of Finance told us were so valuable for the people of Canada, and which, as he said, the government gave out of the generosity of their heart. I am told that twenty more woollen mills have gone out of operation within the last year and that in all there are 73 fewer mills now operating in Canada than there were when the British preference came into force. The operatives in these mills have been thrown out of employment and the bread winners have had to find employment elsewhere. We admit into this country free of duty, or at a nominal duty, from 5,000,000 pounds to 12,000,000 pounds of wool and over 2,000,000 pounds of yarn every year which would have been produced in Canada had we kept

our tariff as we should have kept it against wool, and extended adequate protection to this woollen industry which at one period was developing so rapidly. In addition to that we have 7,000,000 pounds of tops, waste, and rags imported. We threw out of employment over 3,000 operatives on whom probably 15,000 people would be dependent, by virtue of that change in the tariff wjhich was said to lie in the interests of Canada. Why was this unwise policy introduced? For what purpose did the government give that British preference? The Minister of Finance told us it was in the first place to show our generosity and our liberality to the mother country. It is very well to be generous and liberal with what belongs to yourself, but it is not always wise to be liberal with what belongs to other people, and that is what the government did. We were told in the next place by the Minister of Finance that the consumer of clothing in Canada, especially those who purchased the cheaper wearing apparel, would be benefited by this change. Well, I do not dispute that we showed our generosity and liberality, but I do dispute that it has cheapened the cost of clothing to the people of this country. I think I shall be able to prove from the prices quoted by two large establishments in Toronto, that notwithstanding that we brought in over $22,000,000 worth of woollen textile fabrics last year, and notwithstanding that we closed down 73 Canadian mills and at the same time wiped out a valuable market for the wool produced by the farmers of the country, we did not reduce the price of clothing to the poorer people.
Why ? Because the advertisements of these firms tell us plainly that this could not be done. I give the prices of clothing from the files of the Toronto daily papers in 1896, 1905 and 1907. In 1896, throughout November and December, the T. Eaton Company continuously offered ready-made four-button, all wool tweeds, with best Italian cloth lining, sizes 34 to 44, at $6 to $7.50 a suit. At the same time the R. Simpson Company advertised ready-made, all-wool, four-button sack suits of English and Canadian suits, at $5.99, $6.40 and $6.99. In 1905, nine years later, when, according to the Minister of Finance, if his policy had worked out as he seemed to desire and intend, they should have been a great deal cheaper, throughout November and December the T. Eaton Company continuously advertised the same classes of ready-made suits at $10.50, $15 and $18. These figures show that the Minister of Finance's judgment -was bad, that instead of cheapening the cost of these articles to the consumer, that change in the tariff made them very much dearer. In 1905, throughout November and December, the R. Simpson Company advertised the same class of suits at Mr. SPROULE.

How was it that we raised so little wool? Because the crop is not a profitable one and the farmer will not spend his time in raising it. Our country is as well adapted for raising wool as any of these other countries, our population is as large as that of most of them and our area certainly greater. This might be a very profitable industry if wise attention were given to it by the government. The mutton cannot be properly taken to the market because of our transportation arrangements, and, owing to the indifference of the government, we do not secure the better transportation system that we might have and that would enable the producers to send this material to market at prices that would yield much larger returns than at present. The United States produce 330,000,000 pounds of wool against 4,500,000 pounds in Canada. Why? Because their statesmen, years ago, saw the wisdom of fostering the woollen textile industry. This policy was continued steadily until now the

She grows 100,000,000 pounds of wool every pound of which is used in the factories in that country, besides which 557,000,000 pounds of raw wool are imported. And to-day -there are only 2,478,688 sheep in Canada. We had more than that in 1861. We had more sheep in Canada fifteen years ago because sheep-raising was then more proStable than it is to-day. How is it that the farmers of Australia and the Argentine find sheep-raising profitable, although they have no local market whatever for their wool? Their wool is of fine quality, it is wanted abroad, it always commands a high figure and therefore they get a good return for it. At the same time the mutton is sent to the markets of the world in cold storage provided by their government and produces a good return. To give an idea of what

Why? Because our government haye not thought it worth while to provide cold storage facilities so that the products of the farmers may be taken to the markets of the world where they realize a profitable return. The industry of the farmers of Canada is destroyed by the carelessness of the Minister of Agriculture, who proclaims himself to be a farmer and is supposed to be looking after the interests of his fellow farmers. He has failed to do that. The Minister of Finance has struck them heavily on one side and the Minister of Agriculture has struck them on the other. What has this policy of the Finance Minister accomplished for the people of Canada? It has deprived 15,000 or 20,000 Canadians of the means of earning a living and left them in a state of starvation until they were obliged to turn to some other line to earn a living. It has swept away the capital invested in those industries that were running full time when the change was made in the tariff of our country. It has destroyed the machinery which is rusting or has been sold for scrap iron, and every year more and more of these industries are going down until in a few years there will not be one of them left, whereas there were 270 only a few years ago. That policy has destroyed the market furnished by these mills for the wool produced by these farmers. Sheep-raising, one of their best lines of industry, is made unprofitable and therefore they are going out of it at a rapid rate which is indicated by the increased cost of clothing to-day. Instead of getting an increased market and a better price for what he wishes to sell, the market the farmer had is being destroyed and no new market provided in its place. The government killed the Canadian farmers' market in Germany and destroyed the market for consumption at home by those who were engaged in the textile industry, in addition to sacrificing the home market for the wool the farmer raised. done by the Minister of Finance and the other by the Minister of Agriculture.
This was all accomplished by the British preference, Then too, instead of cheapening the goods purchased by the poor people of the country it has increased these over 45 per cent in price. Do the government feel happy over it? Are they satisfied with their policy? Are the people of this^ country satisfied that that policy was a wise one for the country? I do not think they are. Are they grateful to the government for introducing that policy? I do not think they are. What do the farmers of Canada think of that policy? In my judgment they think that the government acted very unwisely, and they would be glad to have some one take up the question in their behalf and introduce a change that will be beneficial. This was accomplished by two members of the cabinet who above all others declared that they were most anxious to do good to two important classes, the poor people of the country who are consumers and the agriculturists who represent so many. The Minister of Finance was going to cheapen their clothing, but he has nearly doubled the price. The Minister of Agriculture was going to do so much for the farmers, being a farmer himself, and he jollies along in the same old slipshod way, he does not get new markets, he only destroys the markets they had, the German market and the home market here in Canada, providing nothing in their place. He did not even provide proper means to lay the products of the farm in the markets of the world and therefore the farmers are obliged to do without beneficial markets where their products might profitably have been sent. In considering these two lines only we have no reason to congratulate either the Finance Minister or the Minister of Agriculture for what they have done for the farmers of Canada or the poor people who are always needy and require to get the cheapest clothing the country can possibly afford. The very men who above all others should be most desirous to help the poor people are the men who have done them the greatest injury and injustice. The man above all others charged with the responsible task of dealing with that question has done nothing, he has destroyed the markets they had and provided no others in return.
I merely make these observations in order to draw the attention of the farmers of the country to what has been done, what accounts for the destruction of their valuable market, what accounts for the fact that sheep-raising is not profitable tc-day. I want to draw the attention as well of the poor people of Canada and to let them know why it is they pay so much more for their clothing, about 45 per cent more than in 1897, when this new policy was introduced and put in operation.

Mr. Speaker, in the mother of parliaments as in the parliaments of the five nations, the financial statement or annual budget by the Chancellor of the Exchequer or the Finance Minister as the case may be, is always a theme of interesting discussion both in the House of parliament and out of parliament. In this country where history is being made very rapidly, where the events of today will be counted as ancient history tomorrow, it is not at all surprising that in a peculiar sense the budget of the Finance Minister is looked forward to with interest. I am very glad to-day to be able to say that during the last twelve or thirteen years in this Dominion the budget speech has been looked forward to with feelings of joy, not with feelings of apprehension. The budget to which we listened the other day is perhaps the most magnificent of all the splendid presentations which the able Finance Minister has presented to the Dominion House of Commons. I am delighted to find that the gentleman who preceded me in this discussion pays this compliment to the Finance Minister when he says that the budget is in most respects one to be rejoiced over rather than to be complained of; and yet, like the good cow that gives a fine bucket of milk and then proceeds to kick it over, the hon. gentleman spoiled the good effect of his speech by an adverse criticism which practically put him out of court. To the present Finance Minister is due the existing fiscal policy of this country, under which Canada enjoys, and has so long enjoyed, such great prosperity, and which has enabled him to make the magnificent showing he was able to make on Tuesday last. Now, Sir, I am in a way glad that the two gentlemen who have spoken for the opposition have, at least in their speeches, found more or less fault with the hon. the Finance Minister, and I will tell you why. The speech and the presentation by the Finance Minister are approved by almost every body, and I hold in my hand a Conservative newspaper, the ' Citizen ' of Ottawa, which contains a despatch from Great Britain to the effect that the address there is received with marked favour by capitalists, who predict that the great prosperity of the Dominion is reflected by it, and that this prosperity is likely to increase.	I say
I am rather pleased to have heard the two gentlemen of the opposition speak on this question, one of them an ex-minister of Finance and who would like to be again Minister of Finance and the hon. gentleman who has preceded me (Mr. Sproule) whose heart has been made sick in waiting for an opportunity to be a member of a new government. They have found fault with the presentation of the Finance Minister, and
so saved him from coming under the measure under this menace of the scripture: ' Woe unto that man of whom all men speak well.' Now the budget's presentation not only gives a splendid view of the condition of the business of the nation, but it gives a fair presentation of the social life of the people, and brings to our attention the growth and development of our trade and commerce. Yet it is too bad that even the opposition in this House should feel inclined to criticise the budget speech, and to pour out the vials of their wrath upon the administration as we have heard them do. Now let me suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, though not wishing to be disrespectful to the hon. gentlemen who preceded me, and to the hon. profession to which he belongs in life, I am bound to say that I can account for it on no other ground than that he is suffering from something like mental measles, and is unable fittingly to appreciate the real state of affairs in the Dominion of Canada. I do know that his desire for the treasury benches makes him feel to-day as melancholy as a pelican in the wilderness, as his colleague the other day showed himself to be as ferocious as a bear robbed of her cubs, when he came to think of the position which he now occupies and the position which he would like to occupy in the government of this country.
Now, Sir, the presentation made by the Finance Minister is remarkable in several particulars. First, it noted the fact of the splendid position this Dominion occupied during the panic that occurred in 1907 and 1908, and if we had time this afternoon to institute a comparison as to the effects of that panic on various countries, a panic which was world wide in its operation, you would find that this country resisted the effect of that panic as no other country was able to do. Why, Sir, in the great republic to the south of us, that wealthy and populous nation, what was the state of affairs? Not only was industry paralysed, but money could not be had to carry on the legitimate business of the country. Owing to the wise fiscal policy now prevailing in this country our business community was happily preserved from the disastrous effects which visited the republic. There was ample money for all legitimate business enterprises and business went on with slight interruption. Albeit the revenue of the country was somewhat diminished, and it was not at all surprising that such should be the case. Now, the Finance Minister's splendid speech also noted the fact that the trade and commerce of the country are growing by leaps and bounds. He was able to tell us of an overflowing treasury, of a great recovery in the revenue of the country which would enable the necessary expenditures to be met without

difficulty. He showed us that notwithstanding all the great expenditures that will have to be made upon the National Transcontinental railway, the increase of the public debt would be $2,250,000 less than the expenditure on that, enterprise alone, and the naval expenditures ordinarily applied to capital account would this as would other years be paid out of revenue expenditures and be chargable to capital account?
Now, this is a remarkable condition of affairs in Canada, a very prosperous condition indeed. It is one that might well cause the hon. gentleman who preceded me to ask the question as to how this condition of affairs is to be accounted for. Well, Sir, it is to be accounted for in various ways. I cannot now follow him in all the paths in which he journeyed in trying to ascertain the cause of the country's prosperity. The way in which he tried to explain it, however, was a twice told tale. lie laid emphasis upon the fact that much of the prosperity of the nation is due to the enterprise of the people, is due to the fact that agriculture is flourishing, is due to the fact that work and wages were never better, is due to the fact that we have a splendid industrialism in Canada. I would like to draw the attention of that hon. gentleman and of the House to the fact that all these vast interests in Canada are growing today, they are developing day by day, month by month and year by year. And how is it all to be accounted for? Sir, I think it is largely owing to the fact that we have a sane and sensible fiscal policy, one which not only ministers to the growth in trade and commerce abroad, but which has helped to build up an interprovincial trade which is vastly superior to that which we enjoy from imports and exports. I was glad to-day, in taking up the Ottawa ' Free Press,' to note the splendid influence that the fiscal arrangements of this country are now having upon foreign capital. The Ottawa 'Free Press' of December 15, has a statement from the State Department at Washintgon, noting that $226 500,000 of American capital has been invested in industrial enterprises in Canada, employing Canadian labour, on Canadian so'l, and ministering to the comfort and convenience of the Canadian people. This is a point that is wmrthy of note. When these gentlemen come to discuss the ifs and ands of the prosperity of the day-and I shall go into detail in a moment more fully as to some of the things said by the hon. gentleman who preceded me-I listen in vain for a declaration from them as to what they themselves would do to improve the situation. I had hoped that they would have presented an alternative policy upon which they might have appealed to the Dominion of Canada. But, Sir, had we anything of

the kind presented to us? No, Sir, we had not. They proceed upon the assumption that the government of the day are perfect men, that they are infallible, that they ought not to be expected to err in any single particular. Sir, high as my regard is for the hon. the Premier and the members of his cabinet, I do not claim for them absolute perfection. I do not pretend to say that there is no possibility of errors having been made, but if there have been errors made in the administration, these gentlemen have failed to point them out, and they have failed to show, if there have been errors, what they would do to meet the situation.

May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? Is this policy which this government has been administering during the last twelve years the policy that the right hon. the Prime Minister enunciated in Winnipeg in 1894, when he promised the people that if he were elected to power he would give them free trade as they have it in England?

I am very pleased to say that when the right hon the premier accepted office and opened that new era for Canada in which we are living now, an era of magnificent growth, development and prosperity, he established for this country the fiscal policy under which we have lived until this hour and which admirably meets the requirements of the situation.
May I ask the hon. gentleman what that fiscal policy was?

Is it that hon. gentlemen opposite are without a policy? I know that they were struggling to manufacture a policy. If I remember correctly there was such a thing spoken of as the Halifax platform and we were to have adequate protection, but since the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) refused to be godfather to that policy and since a wet nurse could not be had for it among hon. gentlemen opposite it has faded into the distant past and we no longer hear of the Halifax policy I had expected, therefore, that by. this time, on the eve of the convention which is called ostensibly, J suppose, to unite the party and to give them possibly a leader under whom they can serve, they would have outlined a policy of some kind. But we are quite in the dark as to what these hon. gentlemen wish us to do in that respect. There is nothing positive from that side of the House, nothing statesmanlike, only faultfinding and unsubstantial statements, and if the hon. gentleman will receive it from me his address to-day seemed very much like putting empty buckets down and drawing nothing up. I have simply to say a word in answer to a few of his criticisms

and to point out a few of the mistaken statements and wrong conclusions which he has arrived at from what he would call his argument this afternoon. There are some facts that we ought to know in connection with the history of this Dominion. I want to state openly, unreservedly and boldly that with the coming into power of the hon. the premier there was opened a new era in the Dominion of Canada, the era in which we are living now and one which is likely to continue for a very considerable time, we trust. I want these gentlemen opposite to have it impressed upon their minds that we are living in an era, which is one rejoiced in by all classes and sections of the Dominion of Canada, by three or four dates which I will venture to mention. Has not the year 1896 itself a meaning for them? Have not the years 1900, 1904 and 1908 a meaning for them? These are very impressive mile stones along the line of the history of this country which ought to convince hon. gentlemen opposite that in all of the appeals that have been had to the electorate since the advent to power of the present government until this day the masses of the Canadian people have been shown to be absolutely, with an almost united front, behind the premier and the government which he leads so successfully. There is nothing wonderful in relation to that.
The hon. gentleman who preceded me undertook to speak on behalf of agriculture and in doing so he made a slight comparison as to the prices of agricultural products last year and this. It would almost seem to me, although I had not intended to do so, that the hon. gentleman needs to have told him some very necessary truths, but in order to do that I should have to move the hands on the dial back not a year but probably thirteen years to direct his attention to the orices of agricultural produce, say, in 1896, and in 1909. If he wants a comparison of that kind he may have it. Let me tell him that the price of wheat, for instance, when the Tories were in power was 58 cents a bushel; to-day we are glad to know that it is a dollar a bushel. At that time the farmers eggs were 10 cents a dozen; to-day they are 25 cents a dozen. Then butter was 12 cents a pound; to-day it is worth a shilling a pound. And if he wants to tell me that the exports of dairy products have fallen off I will tell him that so greatly has the population grown, so numerous have the consumers become, so much better has the home market demand been made than the export market demand that we are glad to avail ourselves of it and the farming industry is flourishing accordingly. The farmer will have little regard for the argument of the hon. gentleman if he will ask him to turn out the present government and place himself and his asociates in power. Now, Sir, there is another change that I would like to speak of in relation to Dominion affairs. Let me contrast the condition then and now. I will not harrow the feelings of hon. gentlemen by speaking of the state of political corruption that was known to exist in Canada then and of the changed conditions now.
Oh, oh.
The people know it and the people rejoice in it.
Hear, hear.

Hon., gentlemen .pay: 'hear, hear'. In those days it was necessary for the leader of the government to expel from the House of Commons of his own party because of their corrupt acts. To-day we stand behind the ministry which is unimpeachable in its character -

Oh, oh.
Mr. FOWKE, And because of the wise economy and absolute honesty characterizing every department a majority of the people of Canada stand united behind this government and overwhelmingly declare that there is such a difference ad between then and now that they want no more of the then and they want to cling to the now. At that time there were such things as national distress and stagnation all over Canada. To-day you find that agriculture flourished to a marked degree, that where there was but the prairie there are now villages-villages	that have grown to
towns and towns that have grown to metropolitan cities, and you find in the east of this country as well as in the west, in the two older provinces, that a large industrialism has been developed and is developing that was not known then and which is employing hundreds of thousands of men, giving them all the work they can do and at splendid wages too. Work and wages never were so plentiful and so much rejoiced in in Canada as they are to-day, and I will tell you why. It is very largely because of the sane and successful fiscal policy inaugurated in the early days of the present administration and persisted in to this hour. And, one of the greatest blessings that has come to us in connection with the fiscal policy is the very one which that hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) professed to condemn this afternoon, namely the imperial preference. I want to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) now, if he is prepared to recommend to his party that that preference should be withdrawn from the mother country? He will not make such a declaration. I am glad from the political point of view that lie condemned the imperial preference as he did to-day, because the people of Canada have proclaimed time and again that nothing has ever pleased them better than

the manner in which, through the channels of trade and commerce, the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier has linked Canada more thoroughly with the mother country than ever before. Is it that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) is simply to wave the old flag and shout loyalty on the 12th of Julv, and that when he is asked to render substantial service to. Britain and to exhibit some evidence of true imperialism, he will, as he has done to-day, speak against a closer association with the motherland. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) dwelt in feeling terms on the woollen industry and of the farmers being deprived of a market for their wool.
Now, I happen to have a large woollen industry in my own town, one which was established a few years ago under rather adverse conditions for the firm was not then rich in material wealth. However, they began the industry there and it has grown and grown with the years until at this hour it is one of the finest of its kind in Canada, and has a plant which I suppose is worth not less than $100,000. From employing a few hands it has grown to employing many hands, and, before I came to Ottawa the president of that company said to me: Mr. Fowke, I hope you will do something to get the woollen industry on a better footing than it is at present when you go down to the session. I said to him:	Why Mr. Schofield is not your industry prospering, is it not a growing industry? and he said: Oh, yes, I have nothing to complain of in respect to my particular industry but it is the woollen industry down some where else in some other part of the country. And I said:	I suppose it is one of those industries which has failed to keep pace with the change in events, that has allowed its machinery to become out of date and has not applied proper business methods in order that it might grow and prosper as yours has. I told my electors on the eve of the election that any manufacturer in Canada who could not live and thrive and prosper under the present tariff ought to be allowed to perish and to go out of existence, and the manufacturers present applauded that sentiment. And, Sir, I stand here to applaud it to-day. The British preference has given us an association with the mother country in business such as we did not have before and such as. we have the right to rejoice in now. It is no argument to say that the farmers are not producing sheep and wool to-day. I would like to point out to my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) that the farmers of this country produce that which it is most profitable for them to produce, and that if they can raise cattle and wheat and other cereals, to greater advantage than they can raise sheep, these are the branches of industry they will undertake and the sheep raising will be neglected. I would like to tell the hon. gen-Ma. FOWKE.
tleman further, that there is a large sheep industry in Canada and that it is known to be very profitable. Sheep are raised in this country not so much for wool as for mutton, and the fancy sheep of Canada are exported to the United States and to other parts of the world in large numbers and with great profit to those who raise them. The hon. gentleman attempted to compare Montana with Alberta, and because Alberta happens to be a larger district than Montana he said that sheep should be raised in Alberta even as they are in Montana. Well, I thank Heaven that Alberta is capable of producing something more than sheep, for Montana is not capable of producing anything but sheep. Montana is a country of hills and of valleys and of running water. In this country we do not have to confine our industry to any particular line, for the farmer as well as for the business man industry is diversified, and under the splendid guidance of the Minister of Agriculture we are getting something like intensified farming so that the Canadian farmer is able to make the most out of the calling in which he is engaged. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) quoted from the catalogue of the T. Eaton Company in an attempt to prove that clothing is dearer to-day than it was before the British preference. Of course the idea he was aiming at would refute his own argument because if we had not a tariff against woollen goods, woollen goods ought to be cheaper in Canada than they were before. But he contended they were dearer and he quoted this catalogue to prove it. Now, I want to tell the hon. gentleman the true state of the case in relation to that matter. Cheap clothing can be purchased to-day in Canada as cheaply as ever it could, but I thank this parliament, and I thank this government, and I thank Providence too, for the fact that the people of Canada do not have to wear cheap clothing any more. If they pay higher prices than formerly for their clothing it is because they have the money to buy better clothing. Our people to-day are better fed and better clothed and better housed and have larger bank deposits than was ever possible before Sir Wilfrid Laurier attained power. Sir, I had the pleasure of the acquaintance of the late Mr. Timothy Eaton, the merchant prince of Canada, and in the last conversation but one which I had with him I said: Mr. Eaton, what is the secret of your success in business life? And he said: Why, I have just one motto in my business life and it is this: A fair field and no favour. That was the expression of a true Britisher and a true Canadian, and the Eaton firm to-day is perhaps the largest employer of labour in the province of Ontario, and they minster to the wants and conveniences of the people to a very large extent, and they have succeeded by putting into effect the

principle enunciated by the founder of the firm. I venture to say that if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) will review the catalogue of the T. Eaton Company again he will find that if there is a man who wants cheap garments to-day he can have them just as cheaply as he could ten years ago. But, owing to the prosperity of the country the Eaton firm bring to the attention of the people not the cheaper but the better wares and the people are able and willing to buy them. Speaking from a party point of view I am glad that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) has assailed the British preference because in my judgment there is nothing in connection with the fiscal policy of this government that more commends itself to the people of Canada than the preference given to the mother country in our markets.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?
Yes.

As one who is largely interested in this preferential tariff that he speaks so loudly about and tells of the great advantage it has been to Canada-I have asked this question before but it has never been answered to my satisfaction although perhaps the hon. gentleman will answer it now-I want to know one solitary product of the Dominion of Canada that gets a preference in the old country. In what way does Canada benefit by that preferential tariff? Is there any preference given to any Canadian product to-day in the market of England that was not given to that Canadian product before the preferential tariff came into force?

The hon. member has asked a question. He belongs to a party that talks very loudly about its loyalty to Great Britain. I would like to illustrate its attitude by a story I once heard. At a school gathering in a country district the British flag was placed on the wall in full view of every one present, and one of the speakers commended the teacher for having it there, and drew from it many important lessons in loyalty for the scholars. When he finished, the teacher said: ' I must tell you, Sir, how the flag came to be there; there is a very bad hole in the wall, and it is very dirty anyway, and I put the flag there to hide it.' That is an illustration of the lip-loyalty of the hon. gentlemen who sit opposite, who loudly proclaim their loyalty from the house tops, but who, when it comes to giving concrete example of the fact that Canada stands heart to heart with the motherland, are ready to say:	'Our
interests are here, and even though we would not be greatly hurt by it, we must not take the chance of doing anything for our mother at home.' The present government acted very differently. They said:
'Great Britain is the best market we have for the products of Canada, we wish it ever to be so, we wish to have our trade with you, both for export and import, we want to know you better, to have closer fellowship with you, and to that end the first statesman of Canada gave the preference to the mother country, the result of which is that there is to-day in the British market a sympathetic regard for the products of this country, even though that market is equally open to the products of the whole world. I am glad to know that transportation under this government is keeping pace with the marvellous development of the country, and I am sure the country will approve of what the First Minister has promised to do in a larger way when the finances of the country will warrant it, in the way of deepening the Welland canal, possibly building the Ottawa and Georgian Bay canal, and extending a railway line to Hudson bay. There is nothing too great to expect in that direction, as transportation facilities must be provided if we are to continue to have immigration in the volume in which we have it to-day. In that respect emphasis may be laid upon the fact that we are in a new era. You do not find that the population of Canada is simply stable, that the youth of Canada have to leave for foreign soil to make a living, as was the case formerly. We are not only retaining our own natural increase, but the best people of the United States and the best people of Europe are coming to us, after a searching investigation showing that they axe worthy of admittance to this country. To-day we have an immigration of 150,000 per annum and a revenue of $100,000,000. This is something to rejoice in; but I ask hon. members to contemplate the time, not very far distant, when the immigration will be, not 150,000 a year, but 500,000, and when the revenues of the country will have gone up to 400 or 500 millions. There are gentlemen listening to my voice who will witness these things, which will come because the foundations for such a splendid superstructure are being laid by the present government. The marked difference between former years and the present time is emphasized by the trade and navigation returns. The trade of Canada under the Conservative administration was $239,000,000; last year it amounted to more than $571,000,000, showing an increase of over $332,000,000. I would like next to show very briefly how this government has materially assisted in the production of wealth in this country. The hon. gentleman who preceded me said, what is largely true, that it is by bringing brain and brawn into contact with the forces of mother nature, and compelling her to yield up her treasures that we get the advantages that we possess as a growing country

to-day. But not only by the fiscal policy of the government, but by the management of the various departments have the Canadian population been taught the way in which they can hope to make the most of their energies in the production of wealth for their own comfort and convenience, and also for the national growth and development. In no one department is this emphasized more fully than in the Department of Agriculture. The manner in which that department has assisted agriculture is of incalculable value to the agricultural interests of the country, by the experimental farms, by the dissemination of information, by the interchange of animal products with the various provinces. Time would fail me to tell of all the ways, so well known to this House and to the agriculturists of Canada, in which that department has assisted in the growth and development of agriculture. So that this government, through its various departments, is to be credited with the fact that the people of Canada, in their various callings, are so prosperous as they are known to be to-day. I have a great many statistics showing that the products of the farm have increased enormously in value; but I will not tire the House by reading them. They are in the blue-books, and may be seen by everybody. The Minister of the Interior, in his immigration policy, has pursued the policy of preserving this as a white man's country and of holding the public lands for the settlers.
The manner in which the Finance Minister presents the finances and deals with them is a subject of congratulation by all of us. And I am sure, accepting each of these departments as a great business department, I can with confidence ask you to come to a conclusion the exact opposite of that propounded by the ex-Finance Minister (Mr. Foster) the other evening when he said that this is not a business administration. I am glad to believe that on the record they have shown themselves to be a business administration, and I am glad to know that by the business community, the wage-e'arn-ing community, the farming community, the banking community, the government is looked to with confidence in presenting its policies, because it is known to be a business government. Now, I would like, for a moment, to refer to one other department of government, that of Trade and Commerce. The hon. member (Mr. Sproule) who preceded me, asked how Canada's prosperity was to be accounted for? It is to be accounted for in part by the opening up of new markets for the products of Canada. That sort of thing has gone on and has grown with the growth of the government from 1896 to this hour.
Will the hon. member (Mr. Fowke) tell us what new markets have been opened up?

I will. In 1896, this country had only one trade commissioner to represent its interests abroad, and that commissioner was ten thousand miles away in the antipodes where there was comparatively little opportunity for trade and commerce with Canada to develop. Since then, eighteen trade commissioners have been appointed and are now engaged in their several fields, in Australia, British West Indies, China, Cuba, France, Holland, Japan, Mexico, Newfoundland, South Africa, Norway and the United Kingdom. It affords me pleasure to say that I have read correspondence with the department from interested manufacturers in this country, which any member of this_ House has equal opportunity to see, pointing to the fact that the information given to them through the department by the .trade commissioners in the various countries has been beneficial in a very large degree indeed.
Did not we have these markets before?

We had not learned to cultivate these markets before. We are cultivating them now, and I have no doubt that because of the having our trade commissioner in Mexico, the fact that they had last year a small crop of barley has led to our exporting large quantities of that cereal at paying prices from the province of Ontario to that country. Such facts being brought to the attention of the department, and the department in turn directing the attention of the business community of Canada to these facts, is helping to extend and enlarge the trade and commerce of the country in a way alike creditable to the government and profitable to the people engaged in it.
There is another department of which I have not spoken, and yet I wish to speak of it because it is a department, I believe, whose operation will be of special advantage to a very large section of the Canadian community. I wish to commend the government for the creating of the new portfolio, that of Labour, and for the appointment of Mr. King to that portfolio. There has been a great deal of talk in the past about sympathy with the wage-earners, but until the present government came into power very little had been done in a practical way to manifest sincere regard for the benefit and advantage of that class. The wage-earners are beginning to appreciate the fact that the government has manifested its interest in them in a very fitting and practical way, and that it will see to it in the future that the interests of labour

ere fairly and honestly guarded, that the wage-earner shall be entitled to feel that his interests are as sacred as those of any other person of the community and that no opportunity will be given to any one to trespass upon his rights and privileges. And I am very glad to know, in this connection, that the annuities established under the Trade and Commerce Department, and with which the members of this House are more or less familiar, have been planned so that the poor man can make an investment of his savings which will be absolutely secure and profitable to him as well. I am glad to know that so fully are the wage-earners and others of the country taking advantage of the Annuities Branch of the government that no less than $340,000 has been received in premiums in that connection.
If I were to attempt further to answer the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) I should point out that the government are helping forward agriculture and other interests of the county by means of shipping subsidies and in other ways too numerous now to mention. I shall not trespass upon the attention of the House, nor attempt to present the case more fully than I have already done. But there is one other particular in which, with your consent, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say we are constantly reminded that we are living in a new era in this country since 1896. I am glad to be able to point out the fact that the government of the day are builders up of the Dominion of Canada and of all its varied interests so far as a government is able to further those interests. But, in my judgment, there is no more striking evidence of this result than the appreciation of it in the old land as never before, as it is being appreciated by the Canadian people as never before. Is it not the fact that the Canadian people have just begun to know their standing in a national sense? I am glad to realize that under the First Minister of the day a national sentiment has been formed in the Dominion of Canada, and that its evidences are to be seen from sea to sea, and from the region of the North Pole to the international boundary in the south. And I think it is important that we note the fact of the creation and prevalence of the national spirit. I hold in my hand a brief excerpt from a speech made by that great cosmopolite, Andrew Carnegie. I want to show how a gentleman, of his standing can speak of-the Canadian people and to leave it with you, with you whether we may not at all suitable times emphasize the fact that Canada is a nation. Mr. Carnegie, in an address on a remarkable occasion in New York, said:
Who made the American nation? A little more than a century ago who was the American? A puny, miserable colonist, a dependent
of another nation. He was nothing higher, nothing better than a Canadian, a man without a country and therefore little of a man.
I as a native born Canadian rejoice in the fact that no man is longer entitled to speak of this country as a mere colony of Great Britain. I rejoice that we can to-day proclaim that we are one of the five nations which, with the British Isles, go to make up the most magnificent empire the world has ever seen. Sir, that spirit regarding us did not exist prior to 1896 in Great Britain, nor did we possess it to any such extent in this country as we possess it today. Not many .years ago British statesmen were willing to say : We will let the colonies go and one distinguished English statesman is even credited with saying that the colonies are as a weight about the neck of the mother country, dragging her down to sorrow and to woe. To-day what do you find? You find the British statesmen outvying each other in speaking of Canada as she deserves to be spoken of, and, as I have already said, you find the Canadian people of every name and of every nationality to-day rejoicing in the fact that we are a united people and that we are a nation. No longer do we speak of the French Canadian, the Irish Canadian, the Dutch Canadian-we no longer write Canadian with a hyphen. But no matter who we are or where we come from, standing on the free soil of Canada, facing the future as we do and rejoicing in the present as we have a right to do, we proclaim the fact that we are a nation in the true sense of the term and that we intend to live the life of a nation, of a nation of free institutions, of large hopes and of noble aspirations.
I hope I have answered, in a way at any rate, the statement of the hon. gentleman who preceded me and that I have shown that one may with considerable pride and satisfaction stand in his place in this House and voice these sentiments as a supporter of the right, hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and of the government who have so successfully guided the destinies of this Dominion for the last 13 or 14 years and in whom to-day we rejoice as a government which present to this country not only a budget such as that which came to us on Tuesday last, but a policy which continues to make for the greatness and grandeur of the Dominion of Canada and for a closer association with the mother country for a larger place on behalf of this country in the affairs of the great continent of which we form a part, and of the empire to which we are so proud to belong.

Mr. Speaker, I hope the hon. gentleman will pardon me if in what I have to say I do not follow his line of argument; I have

another subject which I prefer to discuss. But should I care to be reminiscent I think I could safely recall an instance in my boyhood when I knew a man who on his own account and of his own notion undertook to preach the doctrine of protection in this country and who when he did that was not only derided but even despised, and that I, his son, have come to an age when, as a member of this House, I have seen, as I see this afternoon, both of the great parties of this country striving one with the other as to which is doing the most toward building up the industries of this country.
