I have waited now for a long time to express my views in regard to the naval defence programme of the government. I waited last session for a good many days for some kind of tangible expression of that policy, and for a number of days this session I have waited for some tangible expression of that policy, and apparently we have got it in this budget speech. It may be that it is the policy, not only of the government, but of the whole House, because I am told that it is to be on the lines of the resolution that was unanimously carried in this House last March; so I suppose we have now got a tangible expression of their policy in the budget speech. Now, when the question of war is concerned, even when the question of defence is concerned, while sentiment has a great deal to do with it, the financial programme is everything. But in this matter of naval defence, whatever may have been the expression from a sentimental point of view, the Canadian people, the world at large, will view our naval defence policy as it is expressed in the budget statement, and a budget statement that deals with war, or even if it only deals with defence, if it has not something preponderating in it, something out of the usual, is not very much of a programme, and that is the opifiion I have been forced to form in regard to the naval defence programme of the government as outlined by the Minister of Finance. All he said in the budget speech which he made the other day was that this government intended, out of the curernt revenue of the country, this year and succeeding years, to carry out their policy with regard to naval- defence. There was to be no extraordinary financial arrangement, there were to be no loans incurred for the purpose of carrying out the naval defence of the country jointly with the empire, but the government intended, out of the ordinary revenues of the country, to provide a sum sufficient for the Mr. W. F. MACLEAN.
establishment of a Canadian navy. Now, that to my mind is altogether insufficient, it is not what this country ought to do, it is not what the Canadian people expect this government to do for naval defence. Let me read just what is that programme which is to be realized, as the Minister of Finance says, by an ordinary appropriation out of the ordinary revenues of the country:
This House will accordingly approve of any expenditure designed to promote the speedy organization of a Canadian naval service, in co-operation with and in close relation to the imperial navy, along the lines suggested by the admiralty at the last imperial conference, and in sympathy with the view that the naval supremacy of Britain is essential to the security of commerce, the safety of the empire, and the peace of the world.
Now, I say that if that programme is to be realized by an ordinary grant towards the establishment of a Canadian navy, it is not what this country is bound by its duty to do, and it is not what the people of this country expect parliament and expect the government to do in that matter. If the House will pardon me for a moment, I would like to refer to a statement I made in this House not so long ago, following the right hon. gentleman who leads this House, a statement wherein I tried to show that Canada was an essential, an integral part of the British empire. The right hon. gentleman put it in his way by saying that we were not only Canadians, but we were British; I put it in somewhat another way by reading from the constitutional Act of this country, namely, the British North America Act, wherein it was declared that the parliament of Great Britain created this Dominion of Canada, that the Queen was the head of it, that the Governor-General represented the Queen, and that the oath we all took, whether in connection with legislation or defence, was one of loyalty to the empire, and that we were in every sense of the term an integral part of the empire. From that I drew the conclusion that if we were of the empire and under the British Crown as intimately as we are, and that if we were British as well as Canadians, then it was our duty to do something substantial in connection with the defence of that empire and its Crown. Now, what is it we were asked to do? We were asked to do something, and I propose to read one or two sentences from the proceedings of the last imperial conference in relation to that matter. The British government was represented by Lord Tweed-mouth, who was first lord of the Admiralty, and in addressing the conference he said:
We welcome you, and we ask you to take some leading part in making more complete than it is at present the naval defence of the empire. . . . The only reservation that the

admiralty desire to make is, that they claim to have the charge of the strategical questions which are necessarily involved in naval defence, to hold command of the naval forces of the country, and to arrange the distribution of ships in the best possible manner to resist attack and to defend the empire at large, whether it be our own islands or the Dominions beyond the seas. We thoroughly recognize that we are responsible for that defence. We want you to help us in that defence. We want you to give us all the assistance you can, but we do not come to you as beggars; we gladly take all that you can give us, but at the same time, if you are not inclined to give us the help that we hope to have from you, we acknowledge our absolute obligation to defend the King's dominions across the seas to the best of our ability.
Now, there was a distinct invitation to the Canadian government, to all the associated states of the empire, to join in the defence of the empire. We were implored by the mother, it was the call of a* mother to her children, to her sons and daughters, to these new states which have sprung from her loins, it was an invitation to join her in the defence of the empire. It was not merely a statement that you can do so and so if you like, or you need not do anything. There was a direct invitation on the responsibility of the British government to Canada, to Australia, to New Zealand, to South Africa, to all the conferees in that conference to join the mother country in the defence of the empire. That being the case, I say we are bound to give a better answer to that invitation than the proposal that is contained in the resolution which was passed here last session, notwithstanding the fact that it was said to be the unanimous opinion of this House, and is to be the policy of this government and of this House in answer to that invitation. Not only in this official invitation have we been invited to join in the defence of the empire, but there have come friends and kinsmen of ours from across the sea to visit us. One after the other they have come here, some in an official and some in an unofficial capacity. English papers have come here, English opinion has been expressed and in hundreds of ways outside of the official invitation that was given at the conference we have been asked to join in the defence of the empire. People have been looking to Canada all the world over to see what our action is to be not only in regard to the invitation that came from the British government but in regard to the invitation which has been given to us by so many who have visited us and by the English press and speakers on English platforms. So important is this question of naval defence that the budget which has caused so much trouble in England, is, to my mind, a naval defence budget. It is an effort on the part of the government there to provide for naval defence. It is
an effort to raise money for naval defence. The government of the day in England have embarked on an enlarged programme of naval defence and expensive shipbuilding and in order to carry that out they have a budget which is a revenue producing budget based on the idea that the land of the country should pay a greater amount in taxe.s than it nas paid in the past. And they believe that this additional tax should be, in a measure, used for carrying out the naval defence scheme of the home government. Not only that, but the budget programme of the Conservative party there- and this is the question before the English people to-day-is also a naval defence programme. They propose to reform the tariff so as to produce more revenue and in that way to increase the ability of the country to provide for naval defence. England today is busy with her naval defence. The go'vernment of the day have staked all on a programme of social reform and also on a programme that involves .an increased revenue for the country. They have staked everything on that programme which means an increased revenue for naval defence; and the Conservatives in England are risking everything in the struggle for a programme which they declare means tariff reform, therefore, increased revenue and, therefore, increased ability to carry on the defence of the country and to provide, for a greater navy. That is the condition in England and that condition is brought about by the fact that the whole country sees the. peril . ahead. It is no nightmare that the people have when they believe that England's naval supremacy is in danger of being lost. So the whole people of England, whether of the dominant party or the party that seeks ascendancy, are engaged in a great struggle, one with one programme, one with the other, the object of both programmes being, each in its own way, to increase the revenue of the country so that they can provide for naval defence and so that they can maintain what we ought to be glad to join in maintaining-the idea of British supremacy at sea, that Britannia still rules the waves and that she intends to do so. If this is the programme of the mother country and if the mother country has invited us to join in naval defence, I ask is the programme, as outlined by the Minister of Finance in his statement this week, in line with the duty of Canada, or is it in line with the expectation of the people? All that is proposed, as far as I can read it, and I do not think I misstate the minister's position, is that, out of the ordinary revenues of the country, at a time of great emergency, at a time when the empire is in peril, there shall be taken a sum of money each year for the foundation of a Canadian navy.
My contention is that that does not meet

the case, that it is not consonant _ with our duty to the empire, and that it_ is not consonant with what this country is able to do. We are a rich _ country. Why, when I heard the Minister of Finance state the figures the other day I was surprised at his hopefulness in regard to the buoyancy of our revenue. We are a rich country. We are a growing country. We know the great peril at our doors, and when we look at the peril to the empire I say that we are, not doing our duty and that the statement of the Minister of Finance, which I suppose he made as representing the government, does not go as far as it ought to go towards realizing the views of the people in connection with naval defence.
What is it that we can do in this hour of peril? What is it that Canada ought to do at this time when the naval supremacy of the empire is at stake? We should, first of all, declare by a unanimous resolution in the most direct and pointed language, that we are of the empire, that we are glad to be of the empire, that we are behind the mother country in her hour of peril, that the resources of this country are ready to be spent generously in the maintenance of the naval integrity and supremacy of the empire and we should not only say it in words but say it in deeds and say it bv a vote of money-say here, at least, is $10,000,000, or $20,000,000 of the people's money for the immediate construction of one, at least, or two superDreadnoughts. We will not be able to do that by the establishment of a navy of the modest pretensions that have been proposed by the Minister of Finance. If we wish to stand by the empire we must do it now. The peril may be now and to wait for years to establish a navy will do nothing to relieve the situation, will do nothing to show that we really are not only Canadian but that we are prepared now to accept our empire responsibilities. If this is our duty, and I believe it is our duty, not only to declare we are of the empire hut that cur money is freely at the disposal of our mother country towards increasing her supremacy and her line of Dreadnoughts, we ought to do it generously and we ought to do it now. The programme of the Finance Minister certainly does not do that. How would England be thrilled, how would the associated states of the empire be thrilled to-day if the statement came from this House that we had adopted such a measure as a recognition' of our duty? It would thrill the mother country, it would give a warning to those other nations that are, to my mind, seeking to destroy British supremacy at sea.
Is there anything else we can do? Yes, there is something else we can do and we ought to do it now. What is that? Canada not only ought to declare and declare Mr. W. F. MACLEAN.
now that she is of the empire and prepared to give generously of her money for the increase of the fleet of Dreadnoughts, but she ought to say she is prepared to join the associated states in the establishment of a tariff against the produce of foreign nations, a certain percentage of the receipts of such tariff to be applied to a joint system of naval defence. It is in the air. This country, wherever you go, is ringing with this idea of preferential trade and it is in favour of giving some kind of preference. Hon. gentlemen opposite are on record, and it is to their credit and honour, let it be said, they were the first to do it. But it can go much farther. The thing can be made reciprocal and if we could set the example I say it would be the right thing to do. We should do it now and try to begin the realization of this idea not only of reciprocal trade arrangement but the idea that we are prepared to join with the other states of the empire in imnosing a tariff on the products of foreign countries, a percentage of the revenue from such tariff to be set apart and devoted to a scheme of joint naval defence-The programme that I have -outlined will rot interfere in any way with our idea of having a Canadian navy. I am a Canadian; I want to see Canada complete in every -one of the forms of nationhood; I want t-o -see a Canadian navy; I want to see a great ship-building industry in this country; I want to see great docks in this country ; I want to see this country building warships, if necessary. If we are to have them, we ought to build them here, and a policy of that kind is in the air and seems to be in the minds of the government. We do not interfere with that policy if we contribute our just share to the building of Dreadnoughts. That will come. But we in this country have been devoted mainly to the development of our country. We have not been seamen in the sense of a fighting navy. It takes a long time to develop a fighting navy, men who are masters of the art of war at sea. The mother country is competent in that respect. She has the shipyards and the men; all she wants is more ships and more men, and she can get them, but she will get them all the sooner if we show our devotion by giving the money rather than by saying that we think well of the old country and are willing t-o join, if necessary, in her defence. We must show our devotion in deeds, not words; in dollars, not sentiments; and we must do it now and not in the future, when the opportunity t-o save the situation has gone by for ever. The people of Canada are British; they are patriotic; they are prepared to do their just share in anything. They are not parsimonious. They know that British institutions are worth preserving, and Brit-

ish institutions to-day are jeopardized and British supremacy at sea is jeopardized,. If that be the case, and if we are proud of our institutions, and I believe we are; if we are proud of our parliamentary institutions and our liberties, which we have derived from Great Britain, we have them by reason of British connection and because the strong arm pf Britain is behind them. If that peril is on, it is our duty to join in the maintenance of these institutions. Our greatest asset to-day as Canadians is, first of all, our liberty; second, our parliamentary institutions, our free government. The greatest asset of the world at large to-day is British supremacy at sea; and these two things-Canadian liberty and Canadian institutions and British connection, are altogether dependent at the present moment on British supremacy at sea. Canadians recognize this, and if the appeal is made to them, that they should join in maintaining the naval defence of the country, they will respond as one man, and no government need he afraid to give freely and generously, to pledge the credit of the country, for the maintenance of British supremacy at sea at a time when that supremacy is threatened; and we know that if that threat is realized, these British institutions and this liberty of ours will suffer, this British connection of which we are so proud will disappear, and the mother country and the daughter states will pass into a secondary position in the world. The proposal I have made gives plenty of time to carry out the idea of a Canadian navy. Nothing is lost, but the situation is saved probably, and we get the credit, as the other nations will get the credit, of joining with the motherland in defending those institutions, and in maintaining those forms of goverment which we esteem so much. We not only ought to be prompt in doing this, but above all we ought to avoid imposing conditions in what we do. That is the danger of the situation. Some of us say that we not only ought to have a Canadian navy, but that its control ought to be absolutely in Canada.
Now, I cannot agree with that. If there is a policy of naval defence, it must be one of joint naval defence, and it must be by concessions on the part of every one joining in it. British supremacy hereafter is not to be maintained by the various British states working together with each one imposing conditions, but it is to be maintained by concessions all round, by a generous acceptance of the idea that naval strategy and leadership at present is in the motherland and that we are willing and glad to have it there. I altogether disagree with the idea of imposing conditions and making any Canadian naval movement separate and apart from the British movement or that of any of the other .states. It 52
must be a movement of unity, a movement of concessions, and not a discord of conditions imposed by one or another. It must be a unity on the line of concessions, and the leadership must be in the motherland. I say again that I will give way to no man in asserting my Canadianism. I am willing, and the people of this country, I take it, are not only willing to give generously for building Dreadnoughts or super-Dreadnoughts, but are willing to impose some kind of taxation for joint naval defence, and are willing for the present that leadership should be in the mother country, which, by long usage, by the traditions of her people and by her record at sea, is best fitted to maintain it. I read in the newspapers that the western farmer objects to being taxed for Canada assisting in the maintenance of British naval supremacy. I do not think that is so. I think that when the western farmer comes to see that British naval supremacy means for him the English market, that it may mean in a very short time a preference for the products of the western plains in the British market, he will be prepared-I believe today he is prepared

when he understands the question, to vote liberally for this purpose. But he has to be educated in the matter, and we who are in public life and sit in this House have a duty of leadership imposed upon us. It is for us, if what we say in this House and if the resolutions we have passed mean anything, to go to the people and tell them what we think they ought to do and try to persuade them to do it. I know there will be no trouble in the province of Ontario. There is no trouble in my own constituency. I do not believe there is any trouble in the west or in the province of Quebec or in the maritime provinces. Premier Gouin, in Toronto, yesterday, came out as boldly as an man in this country as.an imperialist, a Canadian, a Britisher, saying on behalf of the people of Quebec that they are prepared to assume their part in the maintenance of British supremacy.
From one sea to the other, from the north to the south, that is the feeling of the people of Canada. All that is wanted is intelligent leadership, all that is wanted is a clear-cut declaration which the people can give their assent to, and once that declaration is made the parliament of Canada will be doing its duty and doing what the country expects from it, if it acts promptly. The only democracy in the world to-day is the democracy of England and her daughter states; the only democracy in the world to-day is to be found under the British flag; democracy is a true British institution and it is an institution worth defending. To-day Great Britain is in one of the greatest political crises in her history, but through the flexibility of her political in-

I desire, Mr. Speaker, to join with others who have spoken on this side of the House in congratulating the Minister of Finance upon the splendid budget he has presented to the people of Canada. I believe that in the statement presented, if I may be allowed to use a general expression, honours are even; I believe that Canada is proud of her Finance Minister and I believe that the Finance Minister should be proud of his national constituency. The condition of the country being as my hon. friend the Finance Minister has presented it, we are in the most flourishing and happy condition, a condition which has continued practically from the time this administration took office in 1896. I think my friends opposite are rather retroactive in the speeches they have been delivering during the present session; I believe that there has been a tendency on their part to discuss reminiscences, matters that were settled in the

general election of 1908. And the worst sinner of them all was my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) the former Finance Minister of Canada. We have been told, for instance-and what individual is there of any consequence or importance in Canada who does not know?- that the Quebec bridge dropped info the river. Who does not know that that was a matter of distressing loss of life and of serious financial loss to Canada as well? But do hon. members opposite think for a moment that the people of this country believe that the government were responsible? Do the people believe that the government neglected any part of their duty in accepting the opinions of the engineers who were appointed by them to take charge of the work after most careful precautions to be assured of their reliability and responsibility? But, that the engineers made a mistake, that the bridge would not carry its own Weight, this country is aware, and we here are aware. But I do think that has passed away and that there is no necessity of taking up the time of this House in discussing a matter that has been settled in the general election of not long ago.
There is a true test of this government, and that is its administration of the country's affairs. If we can judge by the results we have seen during the past thirteen years, there is no reason to complain of the advance that has been made in that time by 'this Canada of ours.' I desire for a moment or two, to present to the House a few facts to show the progress which has been made. The first essential to the development of the country is population. If we consider the facts, we shall find a decided advance in that direction. In 1896, Canada had a population of 5,086,061. Taking the figures of the ex-Finance Minister (Mr. Foster) given the other day, the population of Canada at the present time is 7,184,000, an increase in thirteen years of 2,097,945, as against an increase during the twenty-nine years when hon. gentlemen opposite had control of the destinies of Canada, of 1,714,067. And, if we accept the economic computation that each additional citizen is worth $1,000, we find that the wealth, the'producing capital, of the country has been increased to the extent of over $2,000,000,000. Another criterion of the prosperity of the country is to be found in the business of our chartered banks. The stock in our banks in 1896 amounted to $62,498,183, and in 1909 to $97,436,424, an increase in thirteen years of $35,938,241, not taking into calculation the great increase in market value of the stock or the reserves created by each of the banks. During the last thirteen years of the model regime of hon. gentlemen opposite, from 1883 to 1896, there was only the paltry increase of $1,093,629. But as soon as the people of Canada had their eyes opened to the true condi-52*
tion of affairs and accepted the administration we now have in power things improved, and they have been going right along ever since until we have the conditions represented by the budget presented by the Minister of Finance the other day. Still keeping my fingers for a moment on the financial pulse, I find that the savings bank deposits have increased from $61,244,761 in 1896 to $89,384,146 in 1909, a difference of practically $30,000,000. So you will see that there is money in the banks for all purposes yet. If we consider the total bank deposits, we find that in 1896 these amounted to $245,020,143, and in 1909 to $771,043,090, a-difference of over $500,000,000 in the total bank deposits of this contry, brought about by the efficient administration of affairs during this period.

I don't know anything about Kent county, New Brunswick, but if an appropriation has been made for Kent county, it was made in the public interest, or it would not have been made. I have no doubt whatever that my hon. friend will have some difficulty in proving the insinuation he has made at the present time. If we receive a reasonable return for the money spent, if we are getting all the people expect from the expenditure, and if necessity requires that the government should

appropriate a sum here and a sum there, if requirements have been more indicated in one constituency of this country than another, if it is necessary to get an appropriation for a public work or a public building, our hon. friends opposite say that it is done for the purpose of bribing the constituency. Yet my hon. friends will apply to the government of the day for grants for their constituencies and they will not find fault when the government makes the appropriation. But it is a scandal when money is appropriated for a constituency represented by a Liberal, and we are charged with attempting to buy up a constituency according' to the statement of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. They are speaking, and they continuously speak with reproach to the members of the government because of these expenditures. Well, where have they been able to show that any public expenditure has been undertaken that is not required in the best interests of the country? They have been unable to show that any public building has been constructed that has not been required for public purposes. They may say that the government are extravagant for the time being, but I can remind hon. gentlemen opposite that in the city which I have the honour to represent they erected a post office twenty years ago which is absolutely inadequate to the requirements of the business to-day. They not only built a post office, but they had some trouble over the site which they purchased, and they afterwards, to satisfy the urgent demands of rival members of the Conservative party with corner lots to sell, erected a custom house on another property which the government of the day where forced to purchase for the sake of peace in the family. No doubt hon. gentlemen will say, although this is ancient history, that the government did right at that time in building beyond absolutely necessary present requirements. We have the advantage of the difficulties they created in their own party by not only having a custom house but a post office as well. I mention that to show that while it may look to-day as if the government are spending a larger sum than is necessary on the erection of public buildings. I hope that in twenty years from now there is no part of this fair Dominion that will not outlive any building that the government may erect for public purposes. I hope that the Minister of Public Works will go on in the way in the which he is going and erect buildings that will be in keeping with the advance of the country and that he will not be ashamed to look back twenty years from now upon what he has accomplished and that his judgment will not have been found at fault in having led him to erect buildings that had outlived their usefulness.

The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), if I took his words correctly, said that this government had taken from the pockets of the people $922,000,000, and, after endeavouring to create a misleading impression by an insinuating statement before the people of the country, with one sweep of the hand, he asked: What have they to show for it? Let us take one instance alone. The revenue of the Intercolonial railway, thirteen years ago, amounted to $4,000,000. To-day it amounts to about $10,000,000. That would account for $50,000,000 of expenditure alone. Yet, he asks: What have they done with the money? The money has been spent in the improvement of the rolling stock, in the extension and the renewal of the railway, in increased wages to the employees and in betterments. I would ask if this country has not received full value for the $7,000,000 or $8,000,000 which has been expended upon immigration? Have we not received full value for the work which we have undertaken? I see it stated in a newspaper to-day*that 'the farmer, not Fielding' has produced the good times. The man who produced the good times in this country was the man who, thirteen years ago, assumed the full responsibility of the inauguration of a thorough immigration policy. That policy has been of such advantage to Canada that the farmers who have gone to the west have been able to produce the wealth that was spoken of the other day, and it is the man who instituted that immigration policy, who gave to the people of other lands the information which it was absolutely essential to let them have, who distributed broadcast, I suppose upon the doorstep of every farm house in the western United States, pamphlets setting forth the advantages of Canada, to whom must be given the credit in _ large measure for the prosperity we are enjoying to-day. Farmers came from the United States, two or three at a time, saw the great advantages of the west, and to-day we have them coming in hundreds, yes, in thousands, taking up the lands in the western portion of Canada that have proved so valuable, and it is this immigration that has done so much for our country. We have, I repeat, spent $7,000,000 and $8,000,000 in thirteen years. But hon. gentlemen opposite, when they were in power, only spent sufficient to show us that the money was wasted and that no good return came from it. It was, therefore, absolutely necessary to have money expended in a more effective way. The hon. member for North Toronto endeavoured to point out that the $922,000,000 had been expended improperly, or rather wasted. I have shown that $50,000,000 have been expended in connection with the Intercolonial railway. I have shown that $7,000,000 or $8,000,000 have been expended for immigration and

that Canada is having the full benefit and advantages therefrom, and I have shown that hon. gentlemen opposite only spent about enough to be wasted in the time that they were in power. I would like to ask if he thinks the improvements that have been made in our waterways, in our lighthouses, and in our coast line, not including large expenditures f-or services of similar usefulness, that have cost large sums of money have not resulted in advantage to the country? Does he think that the expenditure upon the St. Lawrence channel, which has been made almost as safe for navigation as a small mill pond, is not of general advantage to Canada? Was he justified in making the insinuation that he did make? When we see the Montreal harbour, which has been made an ocean port, when we see Montreal rivalling New York as a grain port, when we see the greatest vessels afloat landing their cargoes in the harbour of Montreal, can my hon. friend or any one else say that the expenditure which has been made upon this harbour has not been for the general advantage of Canada and for the improvement of our shipping facilities? Does he say that the money expended on Toronto harbour-from $500,000 to $750,000-is wasted money? He referred' the other evening to the St. Andrew's rapids. He would hardly make that speech in Winnipeg; at least I am told that he forgot to deliver it when he was in Winnipeg very recently, because we all know that the money that has been expended is of the greatest advantage to the people of Winnipeg and of the tributary district. He pointed to the premier of this country and told him that he was the custodian and president of the board and that the other members of his cabinet were his directors and jointly the custodians of the funds of the people. We know that he is the president of the council and that his colleagues are his directors, and we also know that they are prepared to take the full responsibility of the expenditure they have made. The advantages which the people of this country have derived are greater than the expenditures the government have made. Does my hon. friend say that the $500,000 spent on the western gap of Toronto harbour was money thrown away? If he does, the hon. member foT West Toronto will not agree with him. Will my hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Hughes) say that the money spent on the Trent Valley canal has been wasted?
Does the hon. member want an answer?
Yes.

I will say that this government has been sorely negligent in not expending the full amount in proper time
on that canal. That canal should have been completed long ago. And if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Stratton) would only join me in seeing that the money is expended on the Trent canal instead of on ditches like the Newmarket canal we would accomplish something.

I can tell the hon. gentleman that in the last thirteen years in which the Liberal government has had control of the affairs of this country, they have expended more on the construction of the Trent Valley canal than the party which the hon. member (Mr. Hughes) supports expended during the previous forty years. And as to the Newmarket canal I may tell the hon. member that we have not forgotten there was at one time such a thing as a Haggart ditch otherwise called the Tay canal, and I do not know that to-day I would swap the Newmarket canal for the Haggart ditch. Will the hon. member from St. John say that the money proposed to be expended on improving the harbour of St. John is an improper expenditure? Will the Conservative members who come from the west say that the money that is being expended at Fort William and Port Arthur in making these harbours fit for the accommodation of the growing trade of the west is an expenditure in the wrong direction? Will these hon. gentlemen opposite say that the new piers in connection with the Quebec bridge should not be built? Will they say now that the Grand Trunk Pacific which has cost a great deal and is costing a great deal should not be constructed? We knew when it was undertaken that it would cost a great deal of money, but we believed it was the right thing to do for we knew it would be necessary to provide transportation facilities for the vastly increasing products of the western country. Will hon. gentlemen opposite say that the subsidies to the different provinces of this Dominion which have increased per year five million dollars, is money wasted? I do not think they will. I see by the papers that the premier of Quebec is consulting with the premier of Ontario to-day, and I would surmise that possibly one subject of their conference is that the provinces should ask more from the Dominion treasury. Will hon. gentlemen opposite say that the increased expenditure on the public service, the increased remuneration of employees, is not in the public interest? Will they say that the one and one-half million dollars expended on the militia in the days of the Conservative Tule would be a sufficient expenditure on the militia of Canada to-day? My hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Hughes) knows the condition our military forces were in during the Conservative regime, and he knows that although our militia service is probably not perfect at present, that it is vastly superior to what

it was then. And yet in view of all this the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) rises and sets all these things aside with one sweep of the hand and he asks: What has become of the $922,000,000 expended by this government in twelve and three-quarter years? If time permitted, it could be easily shown that it was well expended and easily justified, the insinuation involved was most unfair. Will any man on the other side of the House say that the Minister of Agriculture has made any bad expenditure in giving to the farmers of Canada the advantages which they now enjoy? Will they say that the Minister of Agriculture did wrong in spending money to provide transportation facilities for the products of the farmers, and for enlarging and improving their markets?
Now, I have not asked the Minister of Agriculture for anything, and I may tell him in advance that I do not want anything, and therefore hon. gentlemen will recognize that I am disinterested in any compliment I may pay him. I will take the liberty of telling the right hon. the Prime Minister that if all the ministers in his cabinet have presided over their departments as acceptably to the people as the Minister of Agriculture has presided over his; if they have displayed, as I am sure they have done, the same anxiety for the public welfare as the Minister of Agriculture has displayed for the welfare of the farmers of Canada, if they have conducted the affairs of the country in as progressive a spirit as the Minister of Agriculture has, then the right hon. gentleman has been happy indeed in the choice of his confreres. And, if the government should see its way to increase the expenditure for the benefit of the farmers of Canada, I think I can safely say that we on this side of the House will give any proposal of that kind our warmest support. Now, let me point out that the fisheries of Canada last year gave a return of $25,451,985, and let me ask these gentlemen opposite if they can honestly complain of the money expended to stimulate that great industry? Will these gentlemen opposite say that the money that has been expended on immigration both by the former Minister of the Interior and the present min ister is money that has not been well spent? Our friends from the west will tell us that fifteen years ago there were large areas of land as barren as the rocks of Muskoka, and which to-day are as productive as any soil in the world, and that as a result of the policy of this government. Will these gentlemen opposite say that the flower of the American farmers who are leaving their homes to the south of the line and flocking into this country are not welcome citizens of Canada?
