migrants came to Canada from the United States, and 700,391 came from all countries. In ten years, from 1898 to 1909, im migrants, cash and effects equivalent to over 200 millions of dollars have come to this country from foreign lands. Is that not a condition of affairs indicating the prosperity which the hon. member for North Toronto could not see about him? Does it not show that the $120,000 spent in 1896 on immigration by the government of that day was only sufficient to be ineffective, whereas in 1907-8, when an immigration policy that was a policy was adopted by the government, $1,074,697 was spent on immigration, and the results have justified the government in adopting an aggressive policy.
We on this side of the House are reproached, and perhaps properly so, for not contributing our fair share towards the defence of the empire, and to remove that reproach the Minister of Finance has placed in the estimates of this year a sum of $3,000,000. Will that be improper use of the public funds? I may again point out to my hon. friend from Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes) how the militia was starved in 1896. In that year there was spent on the militia a little over $1,136,000. They [DOT]were not in a satisfactory condition. The annual drill was inefficient; the brigades throughout the country were in anything but a satisfied condition, but when this government came into power, they adopted a different mode of conducting the militia affairs of the country. They increased the expenditure year after year, until last year it amounted to six and half millions of dollars, and we have to-day a force perhaps os efficient as that of any colony or any country. Some time ago both sides of this House decided upon the beginning of a naval expenditure and upon assuming a share of the imperial burden. Last session a naval resolution was adopted unanimously by the House, but some on the opposite side have deserted our ranks. Some of our ships have sprung a leak; some of them have been foundered on the rock of Dreadnoughts, others on the rock of a cash contribution; and one noble barque has completely foundered in the deep water of no navy at all. There must be a divided opinion among the hon. gentlemen on the opposite side of the House with regard to how far they are prepared to go in a naval de-. fence policy.
On the other side, what is it?

Yes, on the other side. They seem to be very much exercised about what the government policy will be on this matter. The Minister of Finance stated the other day that an appropriation would be made, and we are about to make a consider-

able expenditure in that direction. But we want our friends on the opposite side of the House, if possible, to have their minds made up to some course that will be loyal and patriotic to the empire, and if they do, we are satisfied that they will support the policy of the government when it is brought down.

May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? He has asked this side of the House to support a policy on the naval question, of which he himself is in favour. Will he be kind enough to state to the House what that policy is, if he knows what it is?

My hon. friend has before him the resolution of the House which was adopted unanimously last session, and for which he voted; and before he will be asked to vote on any question of policy, a Bill or resolution will be laid before the House by the government, and hon. members will then be asked to support or oppose that.
May I ask my hon. friend to implement what he has just said by stating whether the policy he has been speaking of is contained in that resolution, or whether he refers to something further?
The policy of the government will be presented at the proper time.
And yet my hon. friend was in favour of it, although he does not know what it is.

I said that the policy of the government when introduced would be such that I hoped hon. gentlemen opposite would have their minds settled and would be able to support it. I have never yet found the government of the day asking their supporters to vote blindly for anything.
They could not do it.

' No, it could not be done. We desire to have some of the money of this country expended in other directions. In the province of Ontario, if I may be allowed to refer to a personal matter, while I was a private member of the local legislature, I made an address on tire budget in which I endeavoured to point out to the people of the province that we had a large territory yet undeveloped and unexplored of which the ordinary member of that House and the ordinary citizen of the country knew practically nothing, and I pressed upon the government the desirability of having a development and exploration policy. The government adopted my view, and. in the following year, when I was a member of the government, I had the pleasure and privilege of helping to put into
force what I had advocated as a private member of the House. We sent about ten exploration parties into what was then known as New Ontario. They returned in the course of a year and reported to the minister that they had discovered a clay belt of about 1,500,000 acres, that they had found pine timber of considerable extent, and great areas of spruce and poplar of immense value as pulp wood to the people of the province.
Then the question arose, how were we going to get into that country? It was decided by the government to build a railway. No one came forward with offers to construct it, and the government of the province undertook the work. This was the first railway constructed by a provincial government in this Dominion, if my memory serves me correctly.	In the construction of
that railway, the object of which was to reach the clay belt and to bring into consumption the pulp wood of the north country, silver was found;-what is now known as Cobalt was one of the results of the building of that road. Since then, the people have had the advantage of about $29,000,000 taken from the mines of the Cobalt district. And my opinion is, Mr. Speaker, that if we spend a little more money in the development of our country, in the exploration of portions that have not yet been explored, we shall make other finds valuable as these in the province of Ontario. We have pulp-wood in this province that is not now available, we have minerals still undiscovered. We know that the route of the Transcontinental is through the rear portion of Quebec and Ontario, and the reports of the Transcontinental commissioners show that there is a vast quantity of agricultural lands in that region. They tell us that the line from Moncton to Winnipeg is divided, into three sections. Section C contains 5,800 square miles, or 3,712,000 acres; section D contains 10,100 square miles, or 6,464,000 acres; section E contains 3,000 square miles, or
1,920,000	acres, a total of 18,900 square miles, or about 12,096,000 acres. And of this sixty per cent is of value as agricultural land. Passing down Sparks street in this city the other day, mv attention was attracted by a photograph in a shop window. It was a photograph of a silver nugget of 2,100 pounds weight. It suggested the great wealth which has yet to be uncovered in this new territory of ours. I am hoping to see-and expecting every day to see-that, in the construction of the Transcontinental railway through Quebec there will be discovered mineral wealth equal to or greater than that we enjoy in the province of Ontario. I am hoping that the forest wealth, agricultural wealth and mineral wealth to be made available will be such as to more than ever attract attention to

our great resources. _ The area in the three sections mentioned from Moncton to Quebec is seven or eight times as large as Prince Edward Island. That is a territory of some importance to the people. And when we consider the great territory now being opened up west of Winnipeg by the Transcontinental, we find that over 200,000,000 acres will be made available for grain-growing. The hon. member for North Toronto stated the other day that in 1900 we had from the west 32,000,000 bushels of grain, in 1907 160,000,000, in 1908, 230,000,000, and in 1909 the crop amounted to 313,000,000 bushels. The hon. gentleman endeavoured to point out that the farmer, not Fielding, had brought these good times. But I would like to ask the hon. member, were he in his seat, who put the farmer in a position to give to Fielding the revenue that gave to the government the opportunity to present the budget we are now discussing? The hon. gentleman says that the increase produced by the farmer is worth $50,000,000 and may be more, and he asks what particular praise and honour are due to the government for that? And I say, the honour is due to the government for their foresight in the administration of our affairs, for adopting a policy when they came into power that has brought about the conditions we see to-day. Praise and honour are due the government for the wise immigration policy they adopted. In 1895-6, we received from Dominion lands $219,326.14. But what did this government receive last year? In 1908-9, our receipts from Dominion lands were $2,175,214.31. In 1900, the product of the west under the government of that day was 32,000,000 bushels. I do not know what it was in 1896; we have no returns to show. But, as I have already said, the crop in 1909 was 313,000,000 bushels. Deduct from this the 32,000,000 bushels produced in 1900, and we find an increase in nine years of 281,000,000 bushels of grain. And if we are able to induce the same influx of population into the west as has been going on-and I hope and believe they will come in far more speedily-we shall be able to demonstrate that which we have said so often, that Canada is the granary of the empire. Hon. members opposite deprecate expenditures; they criticise every appropriation made by the government to carry on the affairs of the country. Well, my experience is that there are no angels in the management of worldly affairs, but I believe the government are doing all they possibly can. They are liable to make mistakes, and the mistakes liable to our common humanity. But, on the other hand, if there are any angels on the other side of the House, they have taken good care to disguise themselves, for I have not	found them

since I had the honour of knowing them or knowing the way in which the country was being conducted under their regime. There is a provision in the estimates of $3,000,000 to assist in the maintenance of the navy, but that is being proposed by the government. I am not in favour personally of contributing any sum of money by way of cash contribution to the imperial defences. I believe that is against Liberal policy and against Liberal principles. I am opposed to that for two reasons. I believe that no British people should provide money to be expended except under their own supervision, that there should be no taxation to be expended by other people. It violates a broad principle that actuates this government and the people of Canada, and I do not believe that the country would be at all satisfied if a contribution were made by this government to the imperial government for the purpose of building Dreadnoughts.
I attempted to show that we still have in this province great mineral wealth, and that in the development of these now unexplored regions, we will be able to show the people of the world that Canada is as rich in minerals and other valuable natural resources, as we are sometimes fond of stating. We do know that the Cobalt district is the richest district of its character, in the world, and I hope that m the country yet undeveloped there will be opportunities for the uncovering of mineral rocks that have been moss covered and weather beaten for ages and that we will have more than one Cobalt district in this country.
Coming to the administration of our natural resources generally, I believe that we should adopt a policy that will give to our own country, all the development it is possible for it to have, that we should manufacture into the completed state all the iron and steel and pulp wood and nickel that it is possible for us to do in this country. By quoting a figure or two, I will be able to show the House-and I am speaking only for myself and not at all discussing the question of any export duty -what amount of money we are permitting to leave our country by allowing our timber to be exported in the condition it now is. At the same time, I believe that that perhaps can be better regulated in another parliament than this. A cord of pulp wood, whether in the tree or on the wharf, is worth from $2 to $7 a cord. In low grade paper, it is worth from $38 to $45 a ton, and when it is made into high grade paper it is worth $50 to $100 per ton. The quantity of pulp wood exported last year was 794,986 cords of a value of $4,356,391, or about $5.75 a cord. If that were made into paper at $50 per ton it would amount

to $37,749,300, a difference of $33,000,000 in favour of having it manufactured into paper in this country. That would be a ninefold increase. If in the next 10 years we exported 1,000,000 cords at $5.75 that would be $57,500,000. Taking the same quantity manufactured into paper at $50 per ton it would realize $513,750,000, a difference in favour of Canada of $462,250,000. That difference represents the gain between exporting raw products and manufacturing them to their completed condition - the employment of labour and industrial gain in the building and operation of machines.
If we take 1,000 feet board measure of pine lumber and have it cut, it would have a value of about $18 to $20 per thousand feet. The labour in that would represent about $7 or $8. Converted into paper, a similar quantity of pulp wood its value would be about $31.50, the labour being about $12. The proportion of investment would be about $5 in a sawmill to $41 in a pulp mill, so that from the point of view of investment of capital, there is an advantage in favour of the pulp mill of about $36. This will demonstrate to the people of this country that if we adopted a policy of having our pulp wood manufactured into paper,-I do not say for the government to do it, that is not my inten-ntion or desire-we would benefit our national industries to an extent almost beyond computation, that in allowing raw pulp wood to be exported to other countries we are sacrificing the great advantage it would be to Canada to have it manufactured here. If we allowed to be exported in the next ten years the proportionate quantity equal to the present export, we should only realize fifty-seven and a half million dollars. If we manufactured at home the same quantity of pulp wood into paper at the small value of $7.50 per ton, it would amount in round numbers to five hundred and fourteen millions of dollars. Deducting fifty-seven millions, the value of the raw material, from the gross value of the manufactured article, we have four hundred and sixty-three million to represent the positive gain to Canada by this manufacture of her pulp wood. I desire further to impresse on the House that our chief natural products, such as silver, nickel, iron and steel, steel being in my judgment a raw material, should, where iit is at all possible, be converted. into the manufactured article within the borders of Canada. I desire to see the equipment of the defensive sea force or, if it is necessary, the offensive sea force, manufactured in this country if it is at all possible. We have in one portion of the province of Ontario to-day, the Collingwood Shipbuilding Company. That company has done and is doing a great deal, and with proper encouragement, might become a
stil more important industry. It can build ships for our inland waters and for our seas as well. The hon. member for South York, this afternoon, endeavoured to make, as he usually does in his newspaper, a scoop. He presented to the IJouse a policy which I wish to discuss. It has been said that in the coal fields of the eastern provinces, we have the steel and the coal lying alongside of each other and I think it was Mr. Schwab, President of the United States steel corporation, who said there was coal and iron lying alongside each other in Nova Scotia, sufficient to last for 100 years. We have the same conditions on the Pacific as on the Atlantic, and we have similar conditions in the intermediate portions of Canada. I would like to see the government of the Dominion endeavour to have created in Canada a ship building industry that will give the people of Canada an opportunity of commencing to build their own fleet, their own navy on the soil' of Canada.
As we have marked our great Transcontinental railway from the Atlantic to the Pacific with steel rails made m Canada, so I hope we shall have a navy with the same brand upon it, ' Made in Canada.' If this can be done, it would be a very satisfactory state of affairs. We see to-day a great Canadian combination of iron and steel capitalists, perhaps the greatest combination that Canada has ever seen, and yet I believe that combination is for the benefit of the people of this country as well as of those more immediately concerned. I hope that the government will call the attention of those great capitalists to the fact that it is possible to establish the nucleus of a ship building industry in this country that will give to our manufacturing establishments an impetus they never had before. The ship building industry of England was not created in a day; it was like Topsy, it ' jest growed,' it was like the British constitution, it was not created, but it grew. I suppose that Great Britain, if it were necessary, could turn out all the Dreadnoughts that she requires. I am not one of those who fear the downfall of England. I am just as loyal a British subject as any other member of this House, and I have no fears of England's bulwarks falling to pieces, and I have no fears that this Dominion and the other colonies will not do the best they can, and will not go as far as the people of this country desire them to go, in assisting in naval and imperial defence. I am satisfied that when the policy of the government is made known, the country will find that the government has done all that it is their duty to do.
There is one other question I desire to touch upon, and that is the expenditure in connection with Crow's Nest Pass railway. When the hon. member for North Toronto 1 was telling what the government had done,

he forgot to say that this government had expended $3,500,000 in endeavouring to give the railway accommodation that is required in the country traversed by the Crow's Nest Pass railway. If he will turn to the customs receipts, he will find that from the territory served by. the Crow's Nest Pass railway the customs receipts have amounted to three times over the cost of that railway, as far as government aid was concerned. I believe this government has done the best they could for the country. Of course they are human, and like every one else they will make mistakes, but I believe they have done the best that could be done. This country is increasing its expenditure, but at the same time it is growing rapidly in wealth, and I think in the main all the expenditure has been justified. I do not know that, having in mind the relations and record of the government in the matter of expenditure of public money for public purposes, I could say anything more suitable in closing than to repeat the remarks made by Sir Charles Tupper at a political meeting in the city from which I come, when he said:
Although this country is increasing its debt, it is being incurred in the erection of those triumphs of peace-in public works that will stand for ages as the monuments of an energetic people who laid the foundation of Canadian nationality amid the wilds of North America.
I am sure that this utterance of Sir Charles Tupper, made thirteen or fourteen years ago, was justified, and would apply with greatly intensified force to the conditions of to-day under the present administration. I think it is the very general belief throughout Canada that we have never had in the history of this country a government that endeavoured more faithfully to act fairly and squarely by all the provinces, by all the varied interests of this country, than the government which we on this side have the pleasure of supporting.

It is not my intention to criticise at any length the speech of the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Stratton). The hon. gentleman strove to make it appear that in the great prosperity and development this country has enjoyed in recent years, the Conservative party had done nothing and that it was all due to the Liberal government. He intimated that the increase in population of this country has been due to the Liberal party, assisted by immigration. Does he really think that the Conservatives of this country have done nothing towards building up this country and towards peopling it? For my part I do not wish to be denied the credit of having done something to promote the prosperity of this country, and I am sure that Mr. STRATTON.
my Conservative constituents also claim credit for having done something to bring about the prosperity which Canada now enjoys. That style of argument in which the hon. gentleman indulged is one well known throughout this country, and has been heard in every schoolhouse during the last eight years. It is just such an argument as one may hear in a corner grocery among politicians who sit around the stove. Sir, I think we have got beyond that, at least in this House and at this day. Now I must make some reference to the claim he and his friends make of having discovered New Ontario. If they discovered New Ontario they were a long time doing it. They were in power since 1873, and only during their last eight years did they make an effort to find out what New Ontario really was. When the Conservative government came into power they found the pulp wood areas parcelled out among a few friends of the government, _ a country equal to several of the smaller kingdoms of the old world, with an area larger than that of Belgium or Denmark, kingdoms containing a population of 3,000,000 or 4,000,000. These pulp wood areas were divided up and held until the change of affairs came. Then the concession was very promptly cancelled and the pulp wood was put on the market and sold to the highest bidder. The same thing is true with respect to the timber areas. Sales of timber were made in the closing days of the Ross administration in large blocks, townships and areas of 36 square miles at prices which did not exceed one third of the prices obtained by the present government by the method of putting timber up in small parcels and allowing the small jobber or mill man to come in, make his bid and get his limit. I venture to say that there was not a limit sold under the Ross regime that brought over $5 a thousand feet. Sales have since been made under the present regime at $13 per thousand feet, with $2 dues added; so that the reference to the methods that prevail in Ontario is not happy.
No timber was sold in Ontario under the Mowat government, the Hardy government or the Ross government except by public tender or public auction.

I would ask the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Gordon) to say if he knows any thing about the burnt lands along Sturgeon river and if they were not parcelled out among the friends of the party and cut under permits. If I chose to take the time I could cite a number of other instances but I do not know that this really belongs to the discussion.
Reference was made again to the Trent Valley canal. This is an old scarred veteran of many an election campaign and

many an election speech. The hon. gentleman was mistaken in saying that more had been done upon that work since the Liberal party obtained power than had been done in forty years by the other party. But, he will bear me out in saying that the Trent Valley improvement was a provincial work and was carried on as a provincial work until quite recently; so that whatever failures or successes were achieved belong not to the old Conservative party alone. Objections have been taken in this House to the Trent Valley canal, but I shall not take up the time of the House in discussing it further than to say that in the estimates this year we find a very considerable sum provided for expenditure upon the Trent Valley canal, but we find nothing for the branch feeder known as the Newmarket canal. It is not unlikely that this has been hiding behind its big brother and so escaped observation. But, if the Newmarket canal is justifiable, and hon. gentleman say that no part of the expenditure can be pointed out as unwarranted, what is to prevent other towns in that vicinity from seeking the same facilities? Remember that these canals are called feeders. The hon Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) will appreciate this phrase-feeders. It represents a branch of the farm stock that is allowed access to the trough day and night; so that those communities that get access to the canals or railways of the country may be well termed feeders because they are upon the public treasury and will be as long as time lasts. I dare say that Aurora, Schomberg and other towns near Newmarket will be glad to have the canal extended to their limits. Doubtless appli cations will be made on the eve of the next election for an expenditure. These people will not be deterred from applying for public money because the distance is too great. They will realize that the longer the canal the greater the expenditure. It is about time we heard some thing about the Georgian bay outlet of the Trent canal. That question has been before the people of North Simcoe and North Ontario for many years, but it will be in order, in about a year, or a year and a half, for engineers to go through there again and set the old farmers guessing whether it is the canal again or whether it is the election.
In discussing the budget, perhaps, like other hon. members, I have found it is a somewhat difficult matter to attempt to master all the details of our fiscal system and I will venture to say that an ordinary member like myself, coming from the com mon walks of life into this House, feels, to a great extent, that in our tariff and our transportation system there are a great many things that are of such a technical character that he cannot very well master all the questions that he would like to discuss intelligently. I acknowledge my in- -
ability to master all these details and I have heard from a great many others that they are in the same position. As this country developes, by the grace of the Liberal party here, not by the efforts of the Conservatives, our tariff will become still more complex. Our transportation problems will become more complex, the social and industrial questions which we have to face will be more pressing and the question has occurred to me if there was not some method by which all these questions that are out of the ordinary character could be discussed by people who had special abilities in that direction. I might venture to suggest to the House a remedy that has occurred to me. If the Liberal party desire to adopt some general scheme of reform would they not apply to the Senate such a reform as would bring into that body talent specially qualified to deal with these more difficult and complex questions? I know that I am trespassing upon dangerous ground. My hands are trembling as I speak upon the subject. I dare not touch it except in this casual way, but would it not be possible to limit the appointment to five, six or seven years and, by a convention between the two parties, make it a condition that the class of men who had made a special study of the problems we have to deal with should be appointed-some of the men who bulk big in the eyes of the people of this country, the big financiers, the big transportation men, and the men who have made a special study of industrial, social and tariff questions that perplex us. These questions could be discussed and threshed out in the upper Chamber and then passed along to this House. In that way we would save a great deal. With reference to our transportation affairs we would save duplication of railways from one end of this country to the other. If we had had the benefit of the advice of such men as Sir Thomas Shaughnessy, Mr. Hays, and Mr. McGuigan it would have prevented the duplication of the Intercolonial Railway and the New Brunswick section of the Grand Trunk Pacific, it would possibly have prevented the duplication and paralleling of tracks all through the west. It certainly would prevent two rival canal schemes traversing the country. I do not know that it is worth while for a member on this side of the House to offer a suggestion to the government, but nevertheless I throw this hint out as to one way in which this parliament and future parliaments can deal with these questions as they come up. Now, the tariff is complicated; we have a minimum tariff, and a maximum tariff, and a free list, and a list of articles upon which taxes may be put on or taken off, and we have the British Preference surtax, and we have treaties with several countries, and when * the ordinary business man tries to under-

stand all this and to apply it to some fluctuation which may have taken place in the trade of the country he finds it incomprehensible. I think our present tariff could be easily simplified and it would be better for every one concerned if it were. Now, the keynote of this discussion has been the $100000,000 budget, and I notice that while the Finance Minister did not take credit for securing all of this vast revenue, his friends and supporters seem inclined to make the people believe that it was the policy of the government which brought about this very prosperous fiscal condition. Well, $100,000,000 is a very large sum of money and it is well worth looking after. The complaint is made by the government and by gentlemen who support them that we on this side find fault, and criticise, and rake up old scandals. Well, we represent a large section of the people of this country, and is it to be thought that the Conservatives in this House are to take no part in the discussion of how this money has been raised and how it should be expended. With the evidence before our eyes that a great deal of this money of the people is wasted, are we to sit here dumb and not criticise the government for its extravagance? No; it is our duty to protest, and I would think very little of the members of an opposition who did not protest in view of such tacts as we have before our eyes. Surely there is ground for our objecting to the manner in which the Minister of Public Works doles out his favours in public buildings. We have spent a great deal of time this session in trying to find out upon what principle grants of this kind are made by the minister, and I think we must conclude that there is- no principle at all unless it be the principle of helping political favourites. We have in the estimates appropriations for buildings in towns with a population of 1,400 and thereabouts, and we know that these tcwns present no very strong claims for such consideration. It is true that they may be very common place towns before the item appears in the estimates, but the moment the Minister of Public Works decides that he is going to bestow his benevolence upon them he finds abundant reasons. Did he not tell us that Parrsboro, Nova Scotia, is quite a nice town, that Wolfville, Nova Scotia, was a very rising town, and that Fairville, New Brunswick, is a very important town which has mills and factories, as if it were something new to us to hear of a town having a mill and a factory. Did he not tell us that Grand Falls had a fine water-power, and that other towns were beautifully located and had fine residences, and that in consequence of these characteristics they were entitled to a public building. But, there are other towns which have all these qualities and more and which do not get public Mr. McCALL.
buildings from the Minister of Public Works. It would seem that the moment the hon. gentleman has decided to grant a sum of money for a building in a certain town he immediately applies his very great abilities to discovering some reason why that town should have a public building, and when the Minister of Public Works gets going in that line he is irresistible. Now, what is the result of all this? A few of my hon. friends around me are expecting public buildings for their towns and these gentlemen are just as meek as possible in the hands of the Minister of Public Works. They are not going to criticise the hon. gentleman while that promise is hanging over them; to use an agricultural expression, they _ are so tame that they will feed out of his hands. We had an exchange of compliments the other night between the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Marshall) and the Minister of Public Works. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Marshall) pointed out that the town of Aylmer in his constituency had a population of 2,500 and a postal revenue of $6,000, and he pressed his claim modestly but firmly, and the Minister of Public Works complimented him that he was not like some of his colleagues who were disposed to criticise unfairly and he thought he ought to do something for the member for East Elgin. Now, do you think the member for East Elgin will criticise the Minister of Public Works while he is waiting for a public building in Aylmer? Not a bit of it. You will find he will stay quiet the rest of this session until he gets the post office, and the same applies to other gentlemen who are sitting near me. Of course, I can speak boldly so far as I am concerned, for, my town has got a post office without any effort on my part. I can hardly believe that it was given solely as a compliment to me, and I rather suspect it was intended to help the other fellow, but be that as it may, we have a public building. Well, Mr. Speaker, in all seriousness this is not a proper condition of things. Would it not be far more honest if a rule were established that when a town had a certain population and gave a certain revenue to the Dominion it would be entitled to a public building without any other consideration than that it was in the public interest to erect a building there? This holding out of a public building as a gift from the minister is altogether improper. I can imagine that possibly next summer the Minister of Public Works will go to Ontario, and he will be invited to the good town of Aylmer, and they will call a holiday, and the band will turn out, and the school children will march, and the band will play ' See the Conquering Hero Comes,' and the children will sing ' the Maple Leaf for Ever,' and speeches will be

made by the mayor and by the minister, and figures will be given as to the prosperity of the town and its factories and industries, and its beautiful location will be described and all that, and then the Minister of Public Works will say: You have made your case good and you shall have a pest office from me, unless indeed you would prefer a wharf or a bridge, or one of these reversible wharfs that will be a bridge if you want it and a wharf if you prefer to have it so, and if there is no water near the town we will give you a wharf in the open field. I repeat that it would be in the interest of the country, and it would add to our dignity as a people, if the public works were bestowed where they are deserved and not as a bait held out by the minister for political support. I have no doubt' that if a rule were established by which when a town arrived at a certain status it would have a public building, my hon. friend from Halton (Mr, Henderson) would claim it as a right to have two or three buildings erected in his county, but at present I question if he dare even criticise the policy of the government, for if he did he knows what his fate would be.
I say again, it is not dignified for this government to spend the people's money for public services in this manner. I earnestly hope that this will receive the attention of the government, and that next session we shall not have to question and cross-examine the whole night to get a definite answer as to what policy prevails in the distribution of public works, and then not get it. With regard to the expenditure of this $100,000,000, I wish to urge respectfully on those who have the expending of this money that no opportunity for scandal be given, but that the money be expended properly. Matters such as we have had discussed in this House this session and last session should not occur under any system of government. I wish to call attention to the sources from which this money comes; it comes through the custom house and the excise office. It comes from men whose hands are knotted and twisted with their daily toil, from men who are stooped with their labours until they will never see the bright sunlight again in the stature of a man; it comes from men working in mines, the forest and the fields, from men working on a railway section for $1.18 a day; it comes from the factory girls who rise in the morning at six o'clock, go two or three miles to their labour, work all day, and return; it comes also from the wrecked homes and the broken men who have paid their part of the tax through the internal revenue. Is it not, then, fair to say that money gathered from the people, and so much of it gathered through stress and toil, should be regarded as a trust of the most sacred character, and be expended in
a way to benefit the people. Bear in mind that about 85 per cent of the people of this country get no other dollars than handmade dollars-dollars which they only obtain by exchanging them for their labour. This fact ought to be of value to those who have the expending of this money. Now, I am not one who is disposed to take a narrow view of this country. I can join with the gentlemen who have spoken in appreciation of the people who came here when this country -was in the days of small things, and I claim the right, with all those who are not of the Liberal faith, to be accorded our fair share in its development, and this I believe the people of this country are willing to accord. There are hopeful signs all along the line. The discussion we had a few days ago regarding those who are attacked by the dread disease of consumption, participated in by men on both sides of the House, revealed the brotherhood of the family-the knowledge that was strong in the hearts of the members of this House, and the responsibility of the strong to protect the weak. The same thing was shown by the efforts of the Department of Labour to adjust the differences between capital and labour, giving, I trust, at all times to the man who toils an opportunity to secure his competency and the things that make his life desirable. We are drawing near to the holiday time, when we are going home to express good-will to our friends and all that it means in our lives. Would it not be well for us to part from here determined when we return in the early days of January, to try to conduct the affairs of the country in a worthy and dignified manner. The spirit expressed by the Minister of Finance at the close of his budget speech will rest with me, as I think it will with all the members of this House, when he said that we all must do our part3 and acquit ourselves bravely as Canadians should.

Mr. Speaker, like other gentlemen who have spoken on this side of the House, I must extend my congratulations to the Minister of Finance on the splendid financial statement which he ha? been able to present to this House on this, the fourteenth occasion tlfat he has had the pleasure and privilege of presenting such a statement. 1 must say that I have been rather surprised at the kind of criticism, if it can be called criticism, which has been directed by hon. members on the other side of the House to the budget speech. I have watched, but watched in vain, for any real criticism of the financial statement for this year. It is true, the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) did deal to a certain extent with the finances of the country; but if you examine his speech closely, you will find that by far the greater part

of it is taken up in going over the history of the government for the last ten or twelve years, and selecting what he calls scandals. Some of the instances he gave were particularly unfortunate from his own point of view. He said that while in the city of. Winnipeg, he had seen St. Andrew's locks, where the government is spending so much money. But when he was in Manitoba, the hon. gentleman did not venture to say anything against the expenditure on the St. Andrew's locks.	.

May I inform the hon. gentleman that Mr. Foster did discuss the St. Andrew's locks in a banquet that was given to him in the Royal Alexandra Hotel.
Mr. W* M. MARTIN. It is quite possible that the hon. member for North Toronto did discuss the St. Andrew's locks, but I venture to say that he did not say anything in Manitoba against the construction of that work.
Exactly what he said on the floor of parliament a few days ago.

The hon. member for North Toronto went farther west, the province of Saskatchewan, and selected for criticism the sale of land to the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company. If the hon. member had carefully examined everything that has taken place in this country during the past twelve or thirteen years, he could not have selected a more unfortunate instance, from his own point of view, for criticism. Let the best dozen or half dozen Tory orators in the country stump the province of Saskatchewan on the question of the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company's land grant, and I venture to say that, if they criticise it, they will not gain a single vote.
What was the contract with the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company? I may state for the benefit of hon. members opposite that, though they do not know it, the fact is that when this government came into power in 1896 every odd-numbered section of surveyed land in the Northwest Territories was tied up to some railway company and out of these lands the company had the right to make their selections. Between Regina and Saskatoon there was an area of 3,500,000 acres out of wlfich the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Valley Railway Company had the right to select 839,000 acres. Railway engineers and valuators were sent over the land, but the company refused to take it on the ground that it did not fulfil the agreement as it was not land fairly fit for settlement. And in 1902 the railway company had threatened to bring suit to compel the government to set apart another 3,500,000 acres out Of which they would have the right to select 839,000 acres. The Saskatchewan Valley Land Company was formed and agreed to buy 839,000 acres out of the odd-numbered Mr. W. M. MARTIN.
sections from the railway company, and they said they wanted also 250,000 acres out of the even-numbered sections. The price that the railway got was $1.65 an acre with no conditions attached. The government agreed to sell to the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company 250,000 acres of even numbered sections at $1 an acre, but on condition that the company should settle 32 homesteaders on every township before the grant should be earned. The first year that company brought in more than enough settlers to satisfy the terms of the grant. Further, the Saskatchewan Valley Land Company is the only instance that can be pointed to in which the present government sold any lands to or had any dealings with a colonization company. More than that, I contend that it was the Sasaktchewan Valley Land Company whose work led to the beginning of the tide of American immigration that has continued to come to this Dominion during the past six or eight years. The hon. member for North Toronto spoke of the reduction of the tariff under the present government, and he spoke with all the sophistry of which he is capable. He said that from 1896 to 1909 the present government had reduced the tariff by 89-100 of 1 per cent. But he did not take into consideration the goods that had been placed on the free list. I submit that it is only fair, in estimating the average duty on goods coming into the country that we should take into consideration non-dutiable as well as dutiable goods. If hon. gentlemen opposite will take the trouble to turn to volume one of the Report of the Department of Trade and Commerce for 1909, page 15, they will find that the average rate of duty on dutiable and non-dutiable goods in i896 was 19.12 per cent and the average rate of duty at present is 16.58 per cent, a reduction of almost 3 per cent on the average of goods coming into this country.

I am sure the hon. member does not wish erroneous figures to go in ' Hansard.' He has made a mistake. What he is talking about is only one class of goods, the dutiable goods, instead of

both classes as referred to by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster).

I have before me the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and I say that the figures I have given are absolutely correct. The figures given by the hon. member for North Toronto do not take into consideration goods that have been placed on the free list, and I say that to make a fair statement of the reduction in the tariff you must take into consideration non-dutiable as well as dutiable goods. On this basis, as I have said, the reduction is almost 3 per cent. This may seem a small reduction, but the amount saved to the people of the country up to and including 1907-I have not the figures for the last two years-was in excess of $50,000,000.
The hon. member for North Toronto also travelled through the west and went over some of the railways in that country. He calls a part of the western country the 'double-track' country'. He says that you can sit at your car window and drop a pea on the track of some competing railway. There are only one or two places that I known of in the western country where there are what may be called parallel railways. Of course, railways may be parallel if one hundred miles apart. But the impression that these hon membes try to convey is that the two railways are not serving different parts of the country. If we consider the country between Winnipeg and Edmonton and take the main lines of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Canadian Pacific, there is not a place where you can say the railways are parallel. It is true that the two lines converge at Portage la Prairie, but it is necessary that they should converge at competing points. They converge again at Saskatoon. And it is true that for some distance west of Saskatoon they run close together. But there is this fact to be remembered that the Grand Trunk Pacific had completed their survey and commenced construction before the Canadian Pacific Railway got there. West of Edmonton again, the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific run close together. But that is made necessary not only by the conformation of the country but by the fact that they both use the Aellowhead Pass to get through the mountains.
Who was there first?

I do not know that that matters. The Canadian Northern was probably constructed first, but the main point is that they are both going to use the Yellowhead Pass. This brings up the question of transportation in the west. I was bold enough to make an assertion here last session and I was sarcastically commented upon by some of the 53
newspapers for saying that the transportation question was the most important question in the west to-day. Well, I risk another sarcastic reference by repeating the statement that the transportation question is the most important question to be dealt with in the west at the present time. It is true we have got practically three transcontinental railroads today, but we now need branch lines to feed these railways. Last year when I spoke in this House in connection with the loan to the Grand Trunk Pacific railway I said the farmers could not get their grain out of the country. The railways did not appear to be prepared to handle the grain, they had not sufficient cars or they were not capable of handling the large production of wheat and other grains. Owing to the railways having provided better facilities this year and also partially to the fact that the farmers have not marketed so much of their crop there has not been any scarcity of cars in Saskatchewan up to the present.
It seems by the returns they have marketed more of the crop.

That is a later report than I have seen. That goes to show only that. the transportation facilities are better than they were last year. I am glad to hear that from my hon. friend because I believe he was one who opposed the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific in the west.
If there is one thing more than another that characterizes the present financial statement and the condition of Canada it is the word ' prosperity.' A great deal has been said about the natural resources of Canada but I believe, and no doubt other members in this House believe that the mineral resources of Canada will gradually become depleted. Our great timber resources are being gradually pushed farther, north by the axe of the lumberman and the ravages of forest fires. Our fisheries, if they have not reached their zenith have almost reached their zenith of production. There will come a time when all our great natural resources will be more or less depleted. When that time comes I believe Canada must resort to agriculture, as some one has said 'the prosperity of a country depends altogether on its basic industries, and in Canada the chief basic industry is agriculture. Has the government, the Department of Agriculture been doing anything towards the assistance and development of that industry in Canada? One thing that has been done has been the establishment of experimental farms.
They were all established before this government came into power.
I was just going to say something about that if the hon. genii EVISED EDITION.
Is the government competing with and rivalling the farmer in producing the dairy products?

The only object is to teach the farmers what can be done with a proper handling of stock which I would say is a very laudable object for the Department of Agriculture to pursue.
With reference particularly to western Canada, I would point out some things that have been done by the Department of Agriculture in recent years to assist the farmers in raising their crops. It is quite true that in western Canada we have a great Mr. W. M. MARTIN.
many new people coming in. A large number of these people had farmed in the east, and they possibly do not need^ the same teaching and the same example in the line of farming as some of the people who came from foreign countries. The American immigrants are on a par with the immigrants who come to western Canada from Ontario, but we have a large number of immigrants coming to Canada from Europe to whom a great deal of good can be done by having proper experimental farms or stations throughout the west. Some ten years ago the Department of Agriculture established v.'hat is known as the Canadian Seed Growlers' Association, and for five years managed that association. Some five years ago it was decided by the department that it would be better to place the association on a similar basis to the various other associations in Canada, so that the management of its affairs might be under the direct control of the seed growers themselves who had identified themselves with it. The department has continued to supply the association, from year to year, with grants and such funds as this association can use. Over 600 farmers, most of them in western Canada, are at present growing seed _ for the Canadian Seed Growers' Association. These farmers are visited yearly by an officer of tire department, and I understand that a great deal of good has been done in improving the variety of seed grown by the farmers in all parts of the country on account of the efforts made by the Seed Growers' Association. I might also refer to the competitions in fields of standing grain which take place every year throughout the west, and also to the provincial seed exhibitions and seed fairs held at different points in western Canada, at almost a hundred points last year, to exhibit seed and give the farmers a chance to get the best seed on the market. I believe, however, that a great deal more could be done by the Department of Agriculture in the west along the line of establishing small experimental stations. These experimental stations could be maintained at a very small cost. .A very small quantity of land would be required, some eighty acres probably, would do for each experimental station, the idea being to make the farms smaller and have more of them so as to give every farmer in the neighbourhood a chance to go and see the most improved methods of agriculture and to learn the proper rotations of crops, the proper method of handling stock and other matters that interest the farmers, and go to build up a prosperous community. Now, in this connection I would like to refer to a statement which I saw in one of the papers the other day, and no doubt other members of this House saw it also. It was a statement made by Mr. James J. Hill, the great rail-

road magnate of the United States. Speaking, of course, of the United States, he said:
Within 20 years 125,000,000 people, and before the middle of the century more than 200,000,000 people must find room and food and employment within the United States. Where are they to live? What are they to do ? By that time our mineral resources will have been so nearly exhausted that the industries related to them must fall into a minor place. By that time it is apparent that our dream of conquest of world markets will be a burst bubble.
He goes on to say:
The government should establish a small model farm on its own land in every rural congressional district, later, perhaps, in every county in the agricultural states. Let the Department of Agriculture show exactly what can be done on a small tract of land by proper cultivation, moderate fertilizing and due location of crops.
I would recommend these sentiments to the Minister of Agriculture and to the other members of this House. I would also like to call attention to an article which appears in the current number of McClure's Magazine entitled ' No deserted farms in Germany.' It shows what Germany has done by a system of intensive cultivation. I do not need to^ say that the west at the present time is scarcely prepared for intensive cultivation; but there are other portions of Canada, particularly of Ontario, that are ready and prepared for a system of intensive cultivation. But the west which is now filling up with new immigrants on new land, is not possibly in a position to adopt puch methods of cultivation. But that time will come, and it may come within the lives of members of this House This article entitled ' No deserted farms in Germany ' says this:
The policy of conservation that made German forestry such a success is applied also to agriculture. As we have stated before. Germany is not at all a land flowing with milk and honey. In enormous parts of northern Germany the soil is decidedly poor. With that of the United States it cannot compare at all. But proper care did wonders. While the methods of farming used by many Americans resulted in the utter decline of good land in a comparatively short time, the farm land of Germany, even though they have been under cultivation for centuries, bring forth rich crops year in and year out.
Then it goes on to make a comparison between the average crop product in the United States and that in Germany, and it cites what Mr. James J. Hill said.
He made the remarkable statement that the soil of America, once the envy of every other country, gave during the ten years beginning with 1896 an average yield of 13-5 bushels of wheat per acre, while Germany 53}
produced 27-6. For the same decade the yield of oats was in America less than 30 bushels, in Germany 46. For barley the figures were 25 against 33, and for rye 15:4 against 24.
The article goes on to argue that the increased production of these lands in Germany, which are said not to compare with the average lands in the United States, is due entirely to the fact that the Germans have embarked upon a system of intensive cultivation. Now that the government will meet with approval in further establishing experimental farms, I think is shown by a statement which I see in an address delivered by one of the ex-presidents of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, who says:
It is indeed a pleasure to note the steps our federal and provincial governments are taking to foster the growth of this important industry, and to establish it upon a sound and economic basis. No one will rejoice more heartily than the manufacturer in the success which has followed the work of the experimental farms. In so far as they have contributed to a better understanding of the scientific side of agriculture, and made it possible to grow two blades of grass where one grew before, they have benefited not alone the farmer, but the entire country. The same is equally true of the encouragement given by the government to agriculture in other ways.
He goes on to mention other efforts made by the various governments and I commend that statement also to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture and of the House generally. There is one other point I would like to refer to in connection with agriculture, and that is the working of the Fruit Marks Act. I do not know whether my experience has been the same as the experience of other western members in regard to the quality of the fruit imported into the western provinces. But I do know that the quality of fruit that has come into the province of Saskatchewan this year, has been beyond anything we ever had before. I believe that a part of that credit is justly due to the rigid method of inspection put in force by the Department of Agriculture, in conformity with the provisions of the Fruit Marks Act. Previous to 1909, there were only three inspectors in the west, one at Winnipeg, one at Calgary and one at Vancouver. The work was then extended last season by the establishment of a new inspector at Regina, whose territory included Moose-jaw, Saskatoon, Prince Albert, Indian Head and other local points. A new inspector was located at Lethbridge and an assistant was appointed at Winnipeg, the Winnipeg district including Kenora, Portage la Prairie, Brandon and other Manitoba towns. There is also this fact, which no doubt will cause satisfaction to hon. members on both sides of this House, namely, that the

shipment of Ontario apples to the prairie provinces was largely increased during the past season. The fruit I refer to when I say that the quality has improved, was not fruit from the state of Washington, hut from British Columbia and Ontario, and in both cases it was better than we ever got in the western provinces before.
Before I resume my seat, I want to say a few words on the question of the immigration policy of the government. The Department of Immigration has recognized the principle that Canada's growth and Canada's prosperity must, to a great extent depend upon the agriculturists, and to that end the department has always favoured the bringing in of men who will take up vacant land in the west and cultivate it. Now I have looked up the records in the Department of the Interior to find the instructions' that were sent by the Commissioner of Immigration to the various agents in the different countries of the world, and I find that the following instructions have been sent out:
1.	Money is expended and administration is exercised with the object of securing immigrants whose purpose in life is to occupy farm lands, either as owners, tenants, or labourers.
2.	Money is voted and administration is exercised with the object of excluding those whose presence in Canada would tend to add to the congestion of our towns and cities.
Immigration effort is made in those countries which are considered most likely to furnish the people coming within the first of the two classes above specified.
Now the countries in which immigration effort is made are Great Britain and Ireland, France, Belgium, Holland, Germany, Denmark, Iceland, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland and the United States, all of which countries can supply to Canada the very best farmers, men who have been brought up to agriculture. Possibly the most important and useful immigrants we have got during the past two years have been coming from the states. We have got a certain amount of immigration from Sweden, and so far as I can judge from the habits of the Swedes, they make the very best settlers in the Canadian Northwest. They cultivate the soil well, they are industrious, they save their money, they make good citizens, and quickly adopt Canadian institutions. The same of course can be said of the immigrants who come from the south of the international boundary. Now one can scarcely estimate the wealth that is brought into Canada year by year by the American immigrants alone. I have here some figures which I would like to commend to the attention of this House in regard to the nationality of the various kinds of immigrants we have been getting during the past two years. I may say, Mr. W. M. MARTIN.
before giving these figures, Mr. Speaker, that I must congratulate many of the hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House on their change of front with respect to our immigration policy. We are getting in this country now an average of nearly 200,000 immigrants or more each year. It is impossible that among this large number there would not be some that we would be better without. We might say that even in our own country there are some people whom we would be better without.
Oh, oh.
I did not refer to anybody on the other side of the House.
It was on that side.

In a growing country like Canada it is necessary that we shall have men who will perform all kinds of labour. The average Canadian who goes to western Canada does not go there to work for some one else. He goes there to make a home for himself, to become independent, to own his own farm and in a great majority of instances Canadians who go from eastern Canada succeed in doing that. We need other men to perform construction work on the railways. You all know the situation that exists in British Columbia, where the Transcontinental railway was practically held up in its construction on account of the fact that they could not get labourers to perform their work. We must have in that western country a large number of men who will perform construction work. We need farmers and

we need the labouring man, and if the Department of Immigration devotes its attention, as it has in the past, to bringing in agriculturists and labouring men, it is performing a duty it owes to Canada and Canada will prosper under such a policy of .immigration. I desire now to give the House some figures with respect to immigration taken from the records of the department. In the year 1894 we actually got 20,829 immigrants; in 1895, 18,790; in 1896, 16,835, and 'so on during the years following until the number has grown to such an extent that in 1907-8 we received 262,469. Why was it that under Conservative rule immigrants did not come to this country? It was not because the Conservative party did not try to get them- in. I really believe that hon. gentlemen opposite worked hard to get immigrants into this country. I am informed, and I believe it is correct, that in 1896 they actually had an officer in Galicia trying to bring to this country the very people whom hon. gentlemen opposite have criticised this government so severely for bringing in. In nine months of the fiscal year 1907 we got 55,791 immigrants from Great Britain, 34,217 from continental Europe, and 34,659 from the United States. In 1907-8 we got 120,182 from Great Britain, 83,957 from continental Europe, and 58,312 from the United States. In the seven months that have passed of the present fiscal year we got 42,295 from Great Britain, 30,184 from continental Europe, and 65,755 from the United States. Let the increase of immigration from the United States continue, because every one of the American settlers brings settlers' effects and money. The value of the effects per capita of the immigrants coming from the United States in the fiscal year 1908-9 is estimated at $998. Taking the total immigration up to the present time at 59,835, it will be seen that these Americans have brought into Canada wealth estimated at $59,712,336.
I think that covers the points for which I rose to address the House and I have only to say in conclusion that I congratulate all the members of this House and the people of this country on the prosperity that characterizes Canada at the present time and I express the hope that the prosperity of future years will be equal to that of the years through which we are just passing.
