We see annually in the estimates a very large sum, I think this year it is $675,000, for the purpose of ice breaking in the St. Lawrence river. Any money that is spent in British Columbia is not going to be spent without producing a return, such as that for ice-breaking, because our ports are open the year round, and for any money spent this government will have a good asset. I can only attribute the attitude with regard to these expenditures to the fact that I suppose no one minister has time to read the blue-books issued by the department of another minister, otherwise they could not justify for one moment the contrasts to which I have drawn their attention. In conclusion, I trust that the government will take this matter into consideration and see fit to make some further appropriations for public works in that province.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I would much prefer answering in English to the remarks uttered by the hon member for Victoria (Mr. Barnard, who has just spoken. However, as I am more familiar with the French language, I hope the House will bear with me while I address it in my native tongue. The discussion of the budget, if I understand aright the rules of parliament, affords an opportunity to review freely the policy of the country under its various aspects, and for that reason its importance is very great. Of course, Canada's policy is that followed by its government, which is for the time being a liberal government. Under a system of representative government such as ours, the task imposed on the leaders is a comprehensive, responsible and difficult one. They are bound to respect the rights of citizens, and if they have a clear understanding of their duties, they feel it incumbent on them to forward the welfare of the community in all spheres of action. In brief, they are called upon to exert all their powers towards insuring the happiness of the inhabitants of Canada as a whole.
What does that happiness consist in? Thinkers, writers, poets, philosophers of all nations, of all times, of all epochs, have agreed in acknowledging that worldly happiness is essentially relative. It embraces an almost infinite variety of forms. Neither should we wonder at this, since happiness is the state of the soul when satisfied, and since the soul, being infinite by nature, is also infinite in its manifestations. Since the opening of this discussion on the budget, human happiness has been considered, more especially . in its relation to money matters. Those who have approved of the policy of the Liberal government have made the welkin ring with the sweet sounds of

the silver and gold pieces gleefully jingling and singing the material prosperity of the country. On the other hand, those who, in the best of worlds play the part of the pessimist, have filled the air with their desperate wailings, not noticing that such wailings find no echo here, no more than in any other part of Canada.
I said that the happiness of a people was a very variable entity. If the happiness of a people consists in wealth, it must consist in wealth under its various forms. What is wealth to the aged man who fears to look ahead, thinking that death lurks near by and calls "to him? What is a million dollars even to the young man replete with health, physical vigour and self-confidence? The young man relies on his strength, has confidence in himself, and looks with confidence to the future. He knows that by dint of energy and ambition he will succeed in conquering all difficulties on the way to happiness, and it is in that happy disposition that his wealth consists, while the old man's wealth consists in the wisdom which he has gained through life from day to day.
What is Canada's particular wealth at the present time? The Dominion has not as yet reached maturity; it is still in its youth, a vigorous youthfulness which betokens a bright future. Such is the Teal wealth of the Dominion. Canada is full of self-reliance, a self-reliance which is not the result of giddiness, of inexperience, but rests on solid ground, for that young Dominion has just tested its strength in a venture which might have proved fatal, but from which we have come out victorious. Two years ago, in 1908, a financial crisis swept as an immense wave over all the nations of the world.
Canada, like every other nation, was to feel the force of it. Would it stand the shock? One well knew that Canada had increased considerably in strength of late years, but so far had met with hardly any but favourable circumstances. How would Canada make use of its strength when confronted with a serious obstacle, with this severe test? That was the question which the government answered in the affirmative, and which the opposition, in their usual 'pessimistic mood, answered negatively. That depression is now over, and of all the countries whose economical life came under our observation and judment, none better than Canada withstood the test. And if I were not afraid my modesty would overshadow my truthfulness, I would even assert that no country under the sun underwent the ordeal better. The hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) gave us a convincing proof of it on Tuesday night. To-day, I say it again, Canada is self-reliant because it knows its strength.
Why is it that Canada in so few years M. ROT.
acquired so much importance? Why is it that Canada .is everywhere known, respected and courted, if I may use the expression? Why is it that those nations having interests at stake with Canada make so much of its opinions and of its understanding of justice? Why is it that young Canada is treated with due respect and fairness in England, in (France and at Washington? The reason is this, and was given by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) himself when he stated that the trustees of the people since 1896 knew their responsibilities and discharged them properly. That is the reason, Sir and the reason is moreover that these trustees understood that their trust consisted not only.of the material wealth of the country, but of the moral and intellectual wealth of its people as well. In fact, no country could take its place among the nations, despite all the riches of the world, unless the heart and mind of its people were developed, as well as its natural resources.
The government had a hard task to fulfil. The programme which it laid down was vast, immense, difficult, but not above its strength, and it has pursued it unceasingly and with undoubted success ever since. In our days, when money cuts such a large figure, the first thing to be done after finding out what unbounded undeveloped wealth Canada had was to find the means to advertise these resources to the world. How did the government (proceed to do that? In the first place, we must recognize that the premier's personality had, as early as 1896, drawn the attention of Europe upon Canada. His masterly eloquence had turned all eyes towards this country But the Prime Minister had also surrounded himself with active, intellgent and clever men in his cabinet, and these soon showed that Canada, from 1896 to 1898, had not been a sleeping country, but a hustling country. Canadian products were to be seen everywhere, in every exhibition, and cn the markets of Britain, France and America. Our commercial agents were met all over Europe, and not only that, but we have seen Canada grant a preference to the British market and upon such conditions as fairly stunned (powerful Germany. Some hon. gentlemen opposite found fault with the British preference. If you narrow down to a mere question of economic proposition, possibly it might, to all appearances, be folly on our part to have given something for nothing. But can it be forgotten that this preference has ensured Canada's economical independence by getting new markets for us, which taught us to straighten up our backs and show our mighty neighbours that we are not dependent upon them, although thev thought they had us at their feet. This would more than indemnify us for what we gave Britain. We must not overlook the fact

that the British market is the most important of all, and that England stands at the head of all nations in that respect. Our introduction to that market, thanks to the preference we' gave Great Britain, has advertised us more extensively even among our rivals. Is it not a magnificent advertisement from a business point of view? What is trade's foremost object, if not to secure customers. And in order to secure such customers, you have to advertise yourself. Thus, Canada in seeking competition on the British market made itself known to the markets of the world. To that 'point of view, the preference would rank among the cleverest political deals of this government.
Having spread Canada's reputation broadcast, having advertised its mining and lumbering resources, something still remained to be done by the government. Wealth does not lie in undeveloped resources. There remained to open up the great Northwest, and the older provinces understood that the best way to recoup themselves of the money lavished upon the Canadian Pacific railway in the Territories was to create there a market for the manufactures of the east. It was then necessary to direct immigrants to these provinces, and it will be this government's everlasting glory that they have initated this stream of immigration in the Northwest. Numberless populations were almost unable to live on the impoverished soil of old Europe. Did it not belong to us to invite them here on our uncultivated fields, rather than allowing them to starve in their native land, while we had absolutely idle farms in our Northwest, on which they could live and acquire some wealth?
The government realized that they were consulting their own interest and at the same time achieving a humanitarian work, when initiating a great movement of immigration to that region.
What happened, Sir? It happened that in every immigrant induced to come over to Canada from Germany, Norway, Austria, France and Great Britain, we had forthwith an agent who, satisfied with his position, wrote to his own friends in the old country and told them what an immense and magnificent country this Canada of ours was and what a happiness it offered to many of their countrymen who starved in their native country.
That active immigration policy has produced great results. We are told that we are too lavish in the expenditure of public money in the Northwest, that the Grand Trunk Pacific is going to cost many millions of dollars.. Quite true. But since we started building this railway, is it not a fact that over one million people have settled upon the vacant lands of the Northwest, and so they already help us to bear
our financial burdens? Is it not true that the millions of bushels of grain produced by these new settlers and which supply our railway companies with freight have already begun meeting the expenditure incurred by Canada in developing that portion of our territory?
I do not intend to speak at any length on these matters, by indulging in too many statistics, though i am free to say that statistics sometimes serve a good purpose in adorning an otherwise arid and uninteresting subject, a fact which has been well illustrated the other day by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance. It would be useless to dilate any further upon the already well known causes of our material prosperity. If the government have joined in the friendly conspiracy of events to make us prosperous from a material standpoint, they have also realized their duty and their mission, by contributing to our intellectual development. And how did they do so, Sir? By readjusting the subsidies granted to the provinces. The. provincial governments, having under the constitution, the control of educational matters are now able to devote larger snms in favour of education. So, the province of Quebec, -to mention a province with which I am more familiar-was enabled by that increased subsidy, to make an additional appropriation of half a million dollars for educational purposes. Schools are being built everywhere. Technical schools are being established-a matter which was mooted, the other day before the House, in the cities of Montreal and Quebec, having at their head devoted teachers and scientists.
I may further mention tne founding in the city of Montreal of a high commercial school. Montreal, it is true, is a city of tire province of Quebec, but it is the commercial metropolis of Canada. This high school will serve a useful purpose in allowing those of our countrymen who wish to take special courses in certain branches of commerce and industry, to receive in that school the scientific training which they need.
As to moral progress, it is a trite saying that a contented man is a virtuous man and that poverty is the mother of all vices. Now, never before did the morality a(f Canada rank higher than nowadays.
When you inspire a man with hope, when you point out the future to him and when, by focussing his eyes on that future, he foresees happiness in store for himself, for his children and his posterity, he shrinks back from crime. Now, in Canada an era of moral progress, so to say, has been ushered in. Therefore I say that the government have fulfilled their mission

and they have acquitted themselves with honor.
True, there is always room for criticism. But this is what must be expected in the work carried out by a political party and this is what is understood by the Canadian people, by our enlightened electorate. Instead of criticising minor details, mistakes which may have been made and which only small minds are prone to criticise you have to take a general view of the achievements of those men, as a whole. A man should be judged in the light of his achievements, as a whole. It is hut fair that a government should be judged in the same way. Should the blunder or mistakes of that government outweigh their good deeds, then it is the duty of the electorate to turn them out, as happened in 1896. When, on the contrary, the sum of their achievements is found to be considerable and their faults are a negligible quantity, the Canadian electors do just what they did in 1900, in 1904 and in 1908: Vote confidence in 'those men who have so well administered the public affairs.
I couid reply in a few words to the statement made a little while ago by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Barnard) about the maritime provinces. He said: You are spending a great deal of money and making large appropriations for New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and yet these provinces yield less revenue than British Columbia which is receiving less than the maritime provinces. I could give to that statement a reply which any intelligent man would understand and it is this: If to-day British Columbia is able to make so much money, it is indebted for it to the Eastern provinces which placed that province in the position which enabled it to realize those gains, and it is but fair that the Eastern provinces should now get compensation for that, expenditure.
But additional argument could be brought forward in connection with the naval question. The government is criticised for having spent $1,000,000 upon the harbour of St. John and $400,000 on the harbour at Halifax, and yet, there is only such and such a tonnage of sea-going vessels passing through those ports. Let us be fair and say that if we made such large expenditures for those ports in order to allow the port of Montreal to develop and assume the importance it is enjoying to-day, why is it that up to 1896, out of the seventeen or eighteen lines of steamships which had been using the St. Lawrence route, only three, namely the Allan line, the Thompson line and the Donaldson line, did really survive?
It is because their trafie was regular during summer only, and a tramp business during winter.

Now, in order to give to the harbour of Montreal the possibility to compete with the ports of New York and Boston, we had only one way to choose, it was to afford a trafie during summer and winter for our lines. After having supplied with modern implements St. John and Halifax we could keep for us a part of the trade going by New York, Portland and Boston. There fore the province of Quebec is concerned in that expenditure, because these three harbours, Montreal, St. John and Halifax are bound up together for summer trafie and the others for winter trafie.
After all what kind of objection has the opposition against this government? Up to the present time I have heard some arguments made during last election. Imagination is the only creating power which remains with our friends opposite. Before the last campaign they had found some scandals relating to the intercolonial or to the North Atlantic Trading Company and others fantasticals. There were dreams from their imagination but those poor dreams were brutally disappointed by the general elections of the 26th of October, 1908. To-day the members of the opposition contemnlate those dreams with tears in their eyes. Let us respect those tears ; they belong perhaps to people stung with remorse. Let the opposition with its sadness and sorrow. Let the dead bury the dead and let the government well alive continue the work of the living.
